subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, June 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-ll, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to speak on the borrowing Bill today. I have heard a lot being said about this particular Bill, the Budget and all the things that have led up to it. It is difficult to speak without repeating much of what has been said before, but one has to really put this whole thing into perspective. Standing on this side of the House it is veiy difficult to say something without being accused of being partisan, but that is fair game.
Let me assure you and all Members of the House, Mr. Speaker, that as I stand on my feet first thing on a Monday morning at 11.16 a.m. to talk about the borrowing Bill, the results that will emanate from the way the Government is doing its business and the effect it will have on my riding and the people in it, need to be summarized one more time for all sides of the House.
I would preface my comments by saying that if they appear to be overly partisan, that certainly was not the original intent. The thread through my presentation, if there is one, will be how this is viewed by rural Canada and what it will mean to the people of my riding of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception who have their own vision of Canada. It is fair that I should be allowed, even compelled, to represent their vision on this very important subject as it will have an effect, not in the short term, but in the long term, not just on the finances and deficit control in this country, but on our Canadian way
Borrowing Authority
of life and, in particular, on our rural Canadian way of life. That very much includes my riding.
There are certain areas on which I would like to focus. First, I would like to give the impression that people have that I have spoken to in the last couple of months. They believe that the Government and the big business community together have a narrowly focused agenda that has been brought out in this Budget and indeed in the Throne Speech itself. Their perception is that what these two have done is to focus solely on the substantial cuts to Government spending, concentrating on defence and cutting out social programs that have been a part of the Canadian way of life for a long time; indeed unemployment insurance since 1940. They believe that there is a joint desire to impose a new massive regressive sales tax on the people of Canada. I can understand their perception. By the way, I believe the perception is entirely correct.
I would like to review some of the things that have been said by some of the spokesmen for the business community. The thread, if there is one, is that there is a lot of talk about the need for cuts in social programs, and a Government response to the Free Trade Agreement. I am not going to tiy to link any of the ills to the Free Trade Agreement. Anything I have to say will have to stand on its own.
However, the belief is that in order to get moving on the things that need to be done by the Government side of the House, it would appear that the level playing field that was discussed so frequently in the free trade discussion and the cutting out of our social programs is very high on the agenda. In fact it is too high on the agenda for my liking. We are already beginning to see the effects of this. One of my concerns is that a lot of my colleagues say that we are not in government and we do not necessarily have the responsibility to come up with the answers. It is my view that the job of the Official Opposition is to criticize and oppose, but I have told my constituents that there are other ways to go about doing business and I am going to suggest some of them here today.
I understand the need for the machinery of government to operate and the need to fuel the economy with big corporations and big business. I am not against big business, I am all for it. However, certain ameliorations, adjustments and improvements should have been considered when this Budget was being put together. I am concerned that the corporations' share of the tax burden

Borrowing Authority
has fallen tremendously in the last 15 or 20 years despite the various tax reforms which I believe were intended to increase corporations' share of the tax burden.
In 1965 personal income taxes made up 30 per cent of Canada's revenue and corporate taxes made up 20 per cent. In 1988 the situation had changed dramatically. Canadians now pay 44 per cent in personal taxes and corporations pay 11 per cent. It is quite a change from 30 and 20 to 44 and 11 and I wonder where it is heading.
There is another aspect of this subject. Last year big business received a total of $8.9 billion in grants and subsidies from the Government. That is hard to believe. According to a Library of Parliament study, which I think is a pretty reputable source, federal subsidies and assistance payments to big business have grown faster in the past 20 years than social program spending. These subsidies and assistance programs increased from less than 1 per cent of the Gross National Product in 1970 to a peak of 2.5 per cent in the mid-1980s. That is an increase of 1.5 per cent of the Gross National Product in 15 years.
There is another aspect of the $8.9 billion that is being paid to big business. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business which represents 80,000 small firms across Canada said recently that a comprehensive deficit reduction program should include, not a small reduction or a big reduction, but the elimination of the grants and pay-outs to big business.
Their report claims that the economic activity which is the direct result of government grants often falls short in the long run. They go on to say that when a big business, or small business for that matter, is the recipient of these hand-outs the result, in fact, is a degradation of the market-place and it provides a competitive disadvantage for those companies which do not receive a hand-out. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business is a reputable organization and is not partisan as far as I know. I would, therefore, take note of that. I know that a lot of people in my riding have read these kinds of things and are asking me why we do not do something with the
$8.9 billion that is being paid to big business which does not seem to be doing what it was meant to do.
The other aspect which concerns a lot of people in my riding, and I am sure all Canadians, is the uncertainty of what will happen with income tax reform. Looming over our heads is a sales tax. We think we know that it is going to be a certain percentage, we believe it is going to be roughly revenue neutral, but the details of the goods and sales tax which is going to be upon us in 1991 are anything but clear.
Recently the Minister of Finance confirmed that we would begin paying a 9 per cent sales tax on almost everything except main food, rent, health care and education. I do not have to remind anyone in Bonavis-ta-Trinity-Conception who is listening to me that this is 9 per cent on top of the existing 12 per cent. This is a 21 per cent tax on anything you buy or any service you have performed.
I remember when Newfoundland joined Confederation in 1949 and a 7 per cent sales tax was imposed. I remember how tremendous and horrific that was and we are now looking at a 25 per cent sales tax. What is that going to do to the people who have enough difficulty buying clothes to put on their children's back as it is?
This tax started out to be revenue neutral, which is an interesting catch phrase. I do not hear nearly as much talk about revenue neutrality now. What does revenue neutral mean? I do not know. I cannot find any description and I have not heard it defined by the Hon. Minister of Finance. In fact his definition seems to be getting a little more flexible as time goes by. I read media reports saying that the tax grab has already started.
The idea was to remove the manufacturers' sales tax which was, I think, 12 per cent before this Budget and is now taking in roughly $13 billion. However, the manufacturers' sales tax has already gone up to 13.5 per cent and is going to take in another couple of billion dollars. Where does this revenue neutrality start?
We are talking about 9 per cent. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that anyone who knows anything about value-added taxes looks at the countries which have involved themselves in this very interesting experiment. They have come up with some very interesting findings. I was given a list of some of the European countries involved. I
June 19, 1989

do not want anyone to look at the record and say that I was misrepresenting the idea, but I would have to say that the value-added tax of which I speak is not the same exactly, but the principle is the same, the intent is the same, and the graduation is the same.
In Denmark the year of introduction was 1967. It started off at 10 per cent. In 1988 it was 22 per cent. It has gone from 10 per cent to 22 per cent. In France the year of introduction was 1968. It started off at 13.6 per cent and is now 18.6 per cent. France has not done too badly. Remember, we are starting off at 9 per cent in 1991. Germany started off in 1968 at 10 per cent and is now at 14 per cent.
In the interest of brevity I will quote only a few more. Britain started in 1973. Do you remember the fuss when they started with the value-added tax over there? It is now up to 15 per cent. Sweden started in 1969 at 11.1 per cent, less than ours, and are up to 23.5 per cent. The list goes on.
The point I am making is that the principle has been established and all we are haggling over now is the price. I fear tremendously the revenue neutrality aspect of this. I have fears of where we will be 10 years from now. What will the 9 per cent grow to be? The European experience is that in 15 years it has roughly doubled. What will that do to us? I am concerned about that as I think we should all be.
There is another aspect which has me veiy worried. I am talking about the general financing of the way we do business in Newfoundland. I do not think it is a surprise to anyone in this House that Newfoundland depends very much on revenue from the transfer payments to the provinces. They amount to 45 cents out of every dollar and very much depends on where you put it and how you look at it.
People on this side of the House have asked what we are worried about because we are getting an increase. Yes, we are getting an increase but we had budgeted for a certain amount and we are getting a lot less. I look, for example, at the transfer payments to the provinces. People on this side of the House ask what I am complaining about because we are going to get more than we got last year.
Borrowing Authority
Yes, we are, but we are not going to get as much as we thought we were going to get. I think in the case of Newfoundland it is the difference from $23 million to $24 million, to $19 million. That is a lot of money when we look at a province which depends on almost 50 per cent of its budget from the federal Government. Over all in Canada to the provinces which depend on regional transfers it is $200 million. That is a lot of money, when it had not been allowed for.
Dealing with ERDAs, the same subject of money from the federal Government to the provinces, my family, my constituents, and my friends have been involved in a lot of the aspects of federal government grants and transfers in the form of the Economic Regional Development Agreements. There is no way in which I can emote, postulate or indicate their importance to Newfoundland.
I am trying to do all I can here. A lot of people, along with me, in the Newfoundland Government and entrepreneurs in Newfoundland are trying to promote tourism. We find that the ERDA, the Economic Regional Development Agreement which was signed lasted for five years in Newfoundland, to the tune of $21 million. Our Minister of Tourism and Development had to return to Newfoundland a couple of weeks ago with the sad news that we are not to get this renewed.
I do not want to sound like somebody from a rural riding of Newfoundland who is always getting up, complaining, and crying that he is not getting enough. I just want our fair share. Tourism in Newfoundland is still in its embryo stages. I think it is going to be big. I hope that I can help it along.
However, when I see these kinds of obstacles standing in front of me and staring me in the face, I have to remind myself that we are behind in tourism development in Newfoundland. Our fair share is perhaps more than what the fair share would have been for any other province.
To begin with, tourism really had not started until about 10 years ago or maybe 15 years ago. It is still in the early stages. We have almost 100 miles, 90-plus miles, separating us from the mainland of Canada. These are two very important considerations which I am sure were eloquently argued by the Minister of Tourism and Development. We still do not have the money. This is one example of our concern about the cut-backs that

Borrowing Authority
have taken place of which Newfoundland is the recipient.
Later I will be speaking on Bill C-21 dealing with unemployment insurance. I do not want to digress into that. In the interest of time, I am sticking to the main point which is the borrowing Bill. In the context of the over-all effect which it will have on my constituents, I could not sit down without bringing to the attention of the House the Job Development Program which is part of the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Even now, before the Act has been put in place, it has had a tremendous effect on my riding. I think it is safe to say that the organization which was represented by the Canada Employment Centres in Newfoundland- and I know I am speaking for my riding-represents about 20 per cent of the economy. That is a lot of money.
In Job Development Strategy in Canada we find that we are losing $53 million. That is $53 million less, which means millions of dollars to my rural riding. This means that jobs will not get done. This means that people who are unemployed will not get jobs. This means that people who would have their incomes raised higher by higher paying jobs will not have that happen.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for Burlington who gave me a list of some of the job opportunities which were there. I reviewed them in fine detail with my constituency office and with many of my constituents. They were quite impressed that in fact some of the jobs have a bearing on my riding in particular. However, two things came out of most of them that would be available in Newfoundland.First, a lot of the jobs were available in Labrador. Of course, people in my riding are not particularly interested in going to Labrador. Second, a lot of jobs in general for Newfoundland are centred in the urban areas, St. John's, Comer Brook, and Grand Falls. While I again thank the Hon. Member for the opportunity to have a look at that and make use of it, which we are doing, unfortunately most of these jobs relating to Job Development Strategy are in urban areas. It is not going to be very helpful to us at all.
Thming to the business of unemployment insurance not changing very much in the sense of not losing jobs, I do not have to say that the unemployment rate in Newfoundland is extremely high. It is around 15 per cent right now. For the rural areas, it is over 20 per cent. I
think the last time I looked at the average, it was 23 per cent, 24 per cent, 25 per cent.
As I wrap up my remarks on this Bill I would like to go on record to say that I am deeply concerned. I represent the deep concern and almost alarm of my riding on the effect that some of these things, which may be well intended, will have on rural Canada and rural Newfoundland.
What are we going to do about it? What could we have done? I think we could have looked at big business. We could have looked at corporations with a minimum tax. A lot of corporations do not pay taxes. We could have had an adjustment period for these changes which are taking place in unemployment insurance. I think that would have improved the situation somewhat. We could have given people more warning.
As far as the goods and services sales tax is concerned, the impact has not really hit people yet. I think we need to have a good look at it. Is it the way to go, or are there other ways?
I did not have an opportunity to speak on the tremendous effect Canadian-wise that the more than fair cuts out of defence are having on my previous colleagues in National Defence. That will be a subject of some separate comments. I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your generosity in allowing me to finish the threads of my thoughts.

Had we another election in Canada today, I expect the same thing would happen to them.
The point of my question is to deal with the ERDA funding which I understand is now up in the air in Newfoundland. That is part of the budget proposals that have been under discussion in this House and that are

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands for that question. Yes, indeed, this was the subject of some great concern while I was over in Newfoundland during the election campaign.
I left Ottawa with the impression that certain ERDA arrangements had not been negotiated or renegotiated as the case may be. I was kind of nonplussed when I arrived in the province because I was told: "No, no, you do not have any worries about that". In fact I was campaigning up in Bonavista North with the now Speaker of the House, the Honourable Tom Lush who represents Bonavista North. I was told: "No, no, don't use that in your campaign because the Premier has already announced that over $80 million had been approved". There was a Labrador agreement. I do not know the exact name of it, but it had to do with Labrador development. The other one was rural and northern development for Newfoundland.
In my riding I have 10 rural development associations. They are in many ways the focal point of activity which gets things going. I was campaigning and talking to the chairman of these committees. They must have thought it strange that I did not bring to bear the fact that these ERDA arrangements to which I spoke earlier this morning had not in fact been negotiated.
Borrowing Authority
Whether it was a mistake or whatever the case may be, when the then Premier of a province, even of another Party, makes a statement that something has been done I accept those things. The people of Newfoundland accepted it. Certainly the people of the rural associations accepted it. They were launching into programs to get things under way again. As we got a little more deeply into the campaign, in discussion with some of the bureaucrats, I was told: "No, no, these have not yet been approved". I find to my disgust and total consternation that when we get into details of the Budget in fact they have not been approved at all.
The Government served notice that it intended to renegotiate these five-year agreements but that has not been done. I spoke of the tourist agreements which cover aquaculture and fishing. I have four or five projects that are waiting now. They have been held up and probably will not go ahead because there is no money. The pot is empty. It has been drained right out.
As far as mining is concerned, I have a man who has a project that can involve 40 people now and when developed can involve 200 people in a part of my riding where unemployment is up to 30 per cent. I have spent a lot of time trying to help him with it. Regional development agreements are not being approved. We have a combination of the new rules for the reprofiling of ACOA, which mean essentially that one cannot get any money if the project is over $200,000. This man is a pretty brave and strong individual. He has not given up, but had he been someone of lesser courage he would have said: "The game is not stacked in my favour this time around". This man is not happy because of regional development agreements and the changes in the rules of ACOA.
I think reprofiling must mean the same as revenue neutral. We have description, definition, and understanding. I wish we could find better words to convey a better understanding of it. My energies will be focused into trying to get these well intentioned agreements into play. Everyone in the business knew exactly what they meant to my riding, to Newfoundland, and to Atlantic Canada. We have the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Those opportunities have now become pipe dreams and lost hopes. People have had projects in for as

much as $3 million, $2 million, $1 million, to help the tourism industry, but now they cannot be done.
I had to give an answer to my hon. friend, perhaps a rather longer one than he had expected. We were very disappointed that we were told yes, then no, and now maybe. Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the Hon. Member in his initial remarks be quite condemnatory of the $8.9 billion he has identified as money going to the large corporate sector from government funds. I concur with him that this does not seem to be something which is necessary.
Some analysts have great difficulty separating out assistance to corporations by size. Could the Hon. Member clarify what he means by pulling away that funding in relation to the criticism that he also had of the Government's attempt to pull away funding from business through ACOA, EPF funding, and the other funding projects about which he has just spoken? Could he tell us what the distinction should be from his Party's point of view and how pulling away the $8.9 billion funding to the very large multinational corporations would assist outlying regions such as Newfoundland or, in my case, Saskatchewan?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I differentiate very much between the two. First, turning to the $8.9 billion, I can tell the Hon. Member that we do not have many corporations in my riding that would get a piece of that $8.9 billion. His point is certainly not lost of me. The money from ACOA which is being reprofiled had the potential of going to people like the gentleman who wanted to start a mine and create 200 jobs. A constituent of mine has been trying for three years to get a small resort hotel in Conception Bay North where we were going to have a lot of extra economic activity from the prison that was going to be built in Harbour Grace. That is gone now and so is the ACOA possibility. There is a big difference.
I would be more inclined to tap that $8.9 billion as part of deficit reduction program than I would to reprofile the ACOA and make it more difficult for people to get anything over $200,000 to help to get the economy in my riding, and I suspect in his riding, off the ground a little bit faster. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on the borrowing Bill. As my Party's spokesperson for international development, I want to take the opportunity to make some comments on the over-all Budget of this Government.
This Budget is a deceptive Budget. The Government is saying one thing and is doing another. For example, the Government has supported the Brundtland commission report for international development and environmental assistance. That report states very clearly how interlinked we are, that we have to think in global terms. We can no longer just think nationally; we must think internationally.
It was with a great deal of hope that we heard this Government was to support those recommendations. This Budget demonstrates that the Government's understanding of those recommendations are very limited because the hardest area hit in this Budget was international development assistance. Almost one-quarter of all the spending cuts made by the federal Government were taken in the Budget for foreign aid. Although Overseas Development Assistance represented only 2.8 per Cent of federal spending in the years 1988-1989, it accounted for 23.3 per cent of the cut-backs for the years 1989-1990.
The dollar figures we are talking about in these budget cuts is $360 million. Many people wonder about cutting and know it has to be cut somewhere. Members on this side of the House have been concerned with the cuts to our social programs. I do not see these cuts as distinct from one another. When we are talking about cuts of that magnitude the Government has an agenda and that is what I want to talk about today.
Domestic cuts and cuts to international development assistance are a fundamental shift in philosophy, a shift to the right to a more free market thinking that fits in with the whole free trade agenda. I know government Members do not like it when we raise this point. They
June 19, 1989

get glazed eyes when we talk about it. However, when we see that this is happening we have to speak out.
The free market agenda is a turning inwards. We are saying: "We are all right. We do not need to worry about those people over there. Somebody else will worry about it". We have to get away from that kind of thinking if our world is to survive. The Government, by saying that it wants to cut the deficit, is falling into that trap of short-term thinking.
We must open our minds and see where the real solutions are to the global problems that confront us as legislators. We need to do more than just speak up in the House. We have to be prepared to change our views and ideas. The situation in our world demands it.
The Government's Budget is in fact a self-imposed structural adjustment. The structural adjustment that has been imposed on developing countries by the International Monetary Fund is one the Government has decided to make on its own through this Budget. It has cut regional development programs and social programs. It is slowly and surely eliminating unemployment insurance benefits. It is privatizing and buying into the market system which the International Monetary Fund is thrusting upon the world, in the vain hope that it will prop up the international banking system.
It is the banking system that has caused much of the grief in this world. With this Budget the Government is not only protecting those banks but is buying into that whole value system of bankers rejecting the people who are the most vulnerable both here in Canada and overseas. They reject those people who do not have a voice, aside from those few of us on this side of the House who have the courage to stand up and say: "No, we know what they are up to. We know their agenda". We are going to talk about it.
We must ask ourselves who is pulling the strings, who will benefit from Canada turning inward. Whoever is pulling the strings is doing it because we will be so worried about our own deficit and our own internal problems that we will be quiet, we will not speak out or criticize when things happen in Central America, Africa, or Indonesia. We will be so focused on our own social strife that we will not criticize those superpowers that are bringing death and destruction overseas.
Borrowing Authority
We know what is going on. We know the agenda and we are not prepared to be quiet about it. We also have to speak out, as has been done very well by many Members on this side of the House, about the social programs that will be affected and the grief and hardship that will bring about here in Canada. These things cannot be distinct. They are all part of the same plan, this monetarist view of the world that has been so destructive.
Canada's wealth and status as one of the G-7 nations and our repeated previous commitments to increase aid contributions indicate the considerable moral responsibility we bear in this suffering world. Canadians have stated their support for international development programs, yet these cuts threaten abandonment of these key commitments, a weakening of our positive role in world affairs, and a loss of moral authority. It is that moral authority, as much as our ability to send money overseas, that is most worrisome.
We have lived on our international reputation, established largely in the 1960s under former Prime Minister Pearson. We have a strong international reputation and we have lived on that capital for a long time. We have not put very much into it. It was with a good deal of hope that last September we heard the Prime Minister say the following before the United Nations:
Increased development assistance, especially to the poorest countries, is another imperative. Canada has just completed a review of its Official Development Assistance policy. We have reset our bearings to improve the quality and increased the quantity of help we give.
He said that on September 29, 1988. That is why I say that this is a deceptive Budget. Six months later, the Government brought down a Budget which cut $360 million from international development assistance. Once again, the Government was saying one thing and doing another. Did the Government not know that it had a deficit problem six months ago? The problem is that an election campaign intervened. This is why people have lost confidence in politicians. They say one thing and do another. We have to change that because we are running out of time. We do not have the time to be able to say one thing and do another.
In 1984 official development assistance equalled .5 per cent of our Gross National Product. For 1989-90 it has been cut back to .43 per cent. We are going backward in a world that has increasing problems. We have lost our moral authority. The Prime Minister's statement to the United Nations, although it did not appear bland at the time, has turned out to be bland because he is not putting any money behind his statement. We thought

Borrowing Authority
that he had some understanding of the recommendations of the Brundtland commission about the view that the world is interdependent and that we in the developed world have some responsibility to address the ills overseas.
There is a self-imposed structural adjustment program in Canada. There are reductions in regional payments. In British Columbia there are reductions in health care payments and the nurses are currently on strike. There have been reductions in post-secondary education. We are now very concerned about possible cuts in the forestry agreements. It all fits into the mode of linear thinking. Lord preserve us from linear thinkers, and there are more than an abundance of them across the way.
We have to understand that foreign aid is not a frill. It is our contribution to a more stable world. We will not buy into the mindset that says that bigger and better armaments will make us more secure. Thinking people have rejected that mindset long ago. If we want a more stable world, we have to be able to reduce the causes of instability. That means we have to eliminate poverty.
A nice glossy document about Canadian international development assistance says that the first priority is the elimination of poverty. Then the Minister responsible has said that we also have to take our share of the cuts. One quarter of the budget cuts is much more than our share of the cuts. The Minister being an apologist for the Budget is something I find most offensive.
We have to understand that Canada has not only a financial obligation, but a moral one. We have to use our credibility. One wonders why we have so much credibility because of the actions that we often take, but we do have it and we should use that international credibility to effect change, to speak courageously at a world forum such as the United Nations, and to follow up those words
with actions. That means not having cuts in the Budget for international development assistance.
We do not understand why Canada's collective obligations to assist those confronted with economic and social disaster should be so extensively abandoned at this time. We do not believe that Canada's own prosperity can be guaranteed in a fortress North America. We believe that our future is secure only if it is linked with development in which the world's majorities participate. This is a philosophy that Canada has had since the 1960s.
We are a small country in the grand scheme of things, but we have enormous international credibility which is withering away with this Budget and with the actions of the Government. It is fitting in with the grand schemes of the superpowers and the confrontation and polarization that we must resist if the world is going to survive. We have to think about stability and not creating more wars, and the poverty that creates wars, and we also have an obligation to attempt to bring prosperity to other people in the world.
We hear many comments about the refugee flood at our gates, and many people saying: "No, we do not want them. They are going to be taking away our jobs". Those refugees do not want to come. They want to stay in their own countries. It is our obligation to assist them to do that by supporting the development work in their own countries. That is what I am saying about linear thinkers, the turning away, the "we will look after ourselves", clutching ourselves and saying that the rest of the world be damned.
This is what we have to reject. In our Party we do reject this. We have a global vision. We are not only talking in response to government polls that Mr. and Mrs. Middle Canadian states such and such and therefore we will do what they say. We have a long-term vision. We want to change and better this world. This Government's Budget is restricting us from doing that.
Not only is this Budget hammering the poor in Canada by reducing the social programs and by eliminating the universality of our long fought for social programs, but it is also hurting the poor overseas, those most vulnerable,

those without a voice. How absolutely immoral and heartless of the Government to cut bilateral food aid. Then it states that CIDA has to take its fair share of the cuts. We are not talking about a fair share here. We are talking about people's lives.
There is a connection between the people who are most affected here and the people overseas. We also have to ask who is benefiting. It is not ordinary people here, and it is not ordinary people overseas. It is the big people in their board rooms who are running things and pulling the strings. We are going to continue to speak out against this in the weeks and months ahead.

No only that, France is licensed specifically to catch cod off the coast of Nova Scotia.
I am not talking about the incidental catches. How incidental can you get, Mr. Speaker? The Russians have
3,000	metric tons of cod. How much do the Japanese have? How much do the Cubans have? How much do the East Germans have? How much do the Faro Islanders have? How much do the Poles have? The Poles catch grey sole. Mr. Speaker, when you go into a restaurant and order sole, it is grey sole. Poland owns its own vessels. The Polish people come over and are given an allocation of that off the East Coast of Canada.
The hon. gentleman then went on to say that we must give by international agreement fish in excess of Canada's needs. Here is where we have a problem. There is no fish in excess of Canada's needs today. There is not one. They call them "underutilized species". The only underutilized species on the East Coast of Canada are fish plant workers and fishermen. They are becoming an endangered species under the Government.

June 19, 1989

hearing this week about misrepresentation of individual community leaders' views on the matter of small rural post offices and the support for Canada Post's new system.
Can the Hon. Member from Gander tell us a little bit about what he is hearing from the real people about the smaller post offices in his constituency?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only thing I am hearing about the smaller post offices in Newfoundland is that they are closing. The only thing we are hearing from the smaller rural post offices in Canada today is that they are closing. They will be replaced by a box in the snow. Imagine getting up on mail day and having to go out and dig your way down to your mail. That is real service, isn't it, Mr. Speaker? That is real service!
Not only that, but a great many communities are even losing that and people will have to go to the next community to receive their mail. Even in the larger communities up here in Ontario that is happening. Now one usually goes into a pharmacy or drug store to pick up one's mail. I can imagine going to the counter to get your mail and the clerk saying: "Just a minute now. I have to serve that fellow over there who wants some toothpaste and other items". That is the level to which service has deteriorated in Canada today. We need a change all right. To restore delivery in Canada we need a change of government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising today to debate the proposed borrowing authority which the Government has put before the House. As the House will know, this comes about because the Government projects a fairly large deficit again, in the area of $30 billion again this year.
The Government has proposed that before the House rises at the end of June it wants to have the authority to borrow up to $24.8 billion in the very predictable event that tax revenue does not come in fast enough to offset the expenditures the Government has committed to make. The Government wants to borrow $24.8 billion with this Bill before us today. This is a very straightforward Bill which includes that and one other clause saying that the Government will have permission to use an unextended borrowing authority to the amount of $3 billion in the next fiscal year.
Therefore, after April 1, 1990, instead of having to come to the House immediately for extra borrowing
Borrowing Authority
authority, it will have $3 billion granted by the House today to spend in the next fiscal year. This policy is induced by the deficit which is being predicted for the coming year in the neighbourhood of $30 billion.
We have come a long way since the end of World War II. I am not sure that it has all been progress, but the goods and services available to the people of this country have probably come about because of technical progress around the world. However, as a country Canada is having some difficulty keeping up. I remind the House that after World War II we were the fourth ranking industrial nation in the world. Only the United States, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.S.R. rated higher than Canada right after World War II in terms of industrial output.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Order. Would the Member for Winnipeg-St. James please sit.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, after World War II Canada was the fourth ranking industrial power in the world, and we are now either twenty-fifth or twenty-sixth, depending upon which ranking one uses. Our influence and power in the world have shrunk considerably and at a very rapid rate.
At the same time we have had some difficulties deciding how we are going to operate our country. For the past eight or nine years we have been shifting to a user pay deregulation mode and have been following an economic philosophy which is probably monetarist in view, following some of the teachings of Milton Friedman and others. This was started by the Liberals and carried on with a vengeance by this Conservative administration which likes to talk a lot about problems it is having with the deficit.
It does have a problem with the deficit. When it came to power it had an accumulated deficit inherited from previous Liberal and Conservative Governments of about $150 billion to $160 billion. It has handled that very well in the five years since then, to the point that the deficit accumulation now ranks somewhere between $320 billion and $350 billion.
In other words, it has more than doubled in approximately four and a half years. This makes a lot of people concerned not just about the deficit but about this Government's ability to operate anything, let alone the Government of this country.

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
We have been hearing that the way out of this deficit will be to cut expenditures. That seems to be the one-eyed view of this Government to handle the deficit situation. Anybody outside of the Government knows that there are two levers which can be used to handle deficits, whether we are running our own finances, operating a business, or operating a Government. We can cut expenditures, yes, but we also have to find out where to get more money if we are having a deficit problem.
The Government made some bad decisions in deciding where it is going to get more money and where it is going to make the cuts. The result has been that not only does the deficit stay approximately where it is and worsens year by year, but it has not been good for the economy.
Previous to the monetarist view of the world, we had a Keynesian view which attempted to show quite conclusively that by handling spending correctly it was possible for government expenditures in fact to increase the economy and make everyone better off. It is all a question of where we put those expenditures and what we do with the money collected from all of us as a collectivity. We have a political problem but it has created a very large economic problem.
The strategy of this and previous federal Governments has been to involve themselves more with large corporate enterprises and to provide assistance to the very large economic entities which exist in this world. We have heard in previous speeches how grants to big corporate business have risen from less than 1 per cent of our Gross National Product in the 1970s to over 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product in the mid-1980s. We do not have any current statistics to the late 1980s, where we are right now, but I would think that it is probably growing even faster at this point.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business represents the small businesses with which most of us in outlying rural ridings deal when we talk to business, It has called on the elimination of these big grants to big business which it estimates run at about $8.9 billion in last year's Budget.
Just the elimination of those kind of grants would reduce the deficit by more than $8 billion. There would be some justification in doing that, just from a point of view of fairness and equity. How can the small business in my riding or another riding, whether it is in rural
Saskatchewan or urban Edmonton, compete side by side with its new reinvestment tax dollars which it has generated.After it has paid 20 cents or 30 cents tax on that dollar, it only has 70-cent or 80-cent dollars for reinvestment purposes.
We are asking small businesses, in case after case, to go head to head in side by side competition against a large multinational corporation that is investing 100-cent dollars because it has not had to pay any income tax on that money at all. We cannot have fair competition with that kind of a tax system. It is time we had a change.
We have been told by this Government and preceding Liberal Governments that we have to have these kind of tax incentives to big business to encourage investment. What kind of investment are we getting and what are they proposing that we should be encouraging?
We heard in speeches from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on down in both Governments, whether it be Liberal or Conservative, that it was to encourage new factories and new institutions that would create new jobs. That sounds all very laudable, but when a tax advantage is applied whether a new business or a new factory is built, or when there is the same tax advantage for taking over an existing one, businesses being by nature conservative and going where they have the sure thing as opposed to some risk, tend to buy each other out. As a consequence in the last decade or so we have had the biggest boom in buy-outs and takeovers that we have seen in our history, all encouraged by the tax system.
This is a tax system which costs the country money, which leads to the deficit, and which causes us to have to come before the House of Commons every year for borrowing authorities that get bigger and bigger. Taxpayers are going to have to pay for it.
If the Government were serious about creating investment, it could use the tax system to achieve that end. Why do we create a tax system which encourages takeover and has a built-in incentive for all participants to create inflationary expectations? Whether it is real estate or the stock market, everybody who is a player knows that if we can just get this stock up or this property up, we will all be slightly better off. Why will we be better off? It is because there will be a nominal value increase. However, we have a tax system which says that on the first $100,000 of capital gain-and these kind of
June 19, 1989

things are capital gains-we do not have to pay any income tax.
Most of the players in the business world are consciously looking for ways to help each other get the price of certain stocks and certain properties up so that they can all take advantage of the tax-free capital gain and walk out with up to $100,000 in the course of their life-time on which they will not have to pay any income tax at all. Does that encourage investment? I do not think so.
What that type of tax system is doing is encouraging inflation, something which the Minister of Finance has said when he defends high interest rates that he is trying to do away with. He said that he is trying to keep inflation down. How is he trying to do that?It is a little laughable, Mr. Speaker, but he is trying to keep it down with a tax system that encourages the value of stocks, bonds, and properties to go up. He is encouraging inflation with an interest policy that encourages interest rates to go ever and ever up.
That becomes a great cost to the small business people in my riding. It becomes a great cost to the individual taxpayer in my riding and across the country. It is counterproductive to the goals which the Government sets for itself.
In other words, when I am able to complete my remarks after the break I will say that the Government is saying one thing and doing a whole host of other things which will make absolutely certain that its goals cannot be achieved. This application for $24.8 billion worth of borrowing authority gives me an opportunity to point this out to the Government, and I hope that it will take note of it.
May I call it one o'clock and complete my remarks later.

subtopic: STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S. O. 31
STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S. O. 31
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR A NETWORK TV STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, New Brunswick is the only province in Canada not to have its own television station that is entirely owned and operated by the English network of the CBC.
Therefore, New Brunswickers must be satisfied with watching English-language CBC programs on CHSJ in Saint John.
Given the French-English mix of New Brunswick's population and the CBC's mandate to unite all Canadians, it does not seem very fair that this province is denied a network station. In fact, this situation is clearly intolerable.

The establishment of a full CBC station in New Brunswick would permit the province to reap benefits beyond the television service. With complete production facilities in the province and more New Brunswick-made shows produced there, the province's artists, actors, technicians and other professionals would be provided with new opportunities which are now closed to them.
Although the CBC has been the victim of drastic budget cuts, the need for an owned and operated station in New Brunswick still exists. All that is needed is for the federal Government to show the political will to make it a reality.

subtopic: AIRLINES
AIRLINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, June 16,1 had the opportunity to represent our Government at the inaugural flight of United Express-Aspen Airways from Denver, Colorado to Grand Forkes, North Dakota to Winnipeg, Manitoba.

June 19, 1989
The role of the Government of Canada in conjunction with the Government of the United States in the approval of the licence for this service is a positive development in the transportation interface between our two countries.
I commend Mr. Don Ringsby and Mr. Don Martins of Aspen Airways for their special efforts in the re-establishment of this program. I would like to congratulate Governor Rommer of Colorado, Governor Sinner of North Dakota and Premier Filmon of Manitoba for their initiative in setting up this regional service.
This licence is not part of the Free Trade Agreement but with the renewal of this air service the business climate between our great countries will no doubt improve even more.

subtopic: RAILWAYS
RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a very important meeting was held this morning on the future of VIA Rail. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) met with the Mayors of Windsor, Toronto, Mississauga, Montreal, Quebec City and, of course, the great city of Hamilton.
The mayors expressed their desire to modernize the Windsor-Quebec corridor with a rapid and potentially profitable service. The Government unfortunately does not see it this way. Cuts to the budget for VIA Rail would likely impact greatly on the development of passenger rail service in the Windsor-Quebec corridor. Commuters will be forced to look for alternatives to train service which would certainly be more costly and damaging to the environment.
For 1988, the number of passengers on the train between Niagara and Toronto was 273,000 people, of which over 33,000 people either got on or off the train at Hamilton. From January 1 to May 31 of this year there were 98,000 passengers on this line. Ridership, Mr. Speaker, is increasing not decreasing. A multi-modal approach makes sense. The solution is to build a highspeed rail network from Windsor to Quebec and ease the congestion of air traffic from Pearson International Airport by incorporating Hamilton Airport.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE
NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prairie farmers who traded used farm machinery in the early 1980s to buy new equipment are still being harassed by Revenue Canada over investment tax credits and the value of trade-ins.
Last year the Department agreed to pay the field cost of a Saskatchewan farmer which would serve as a test case for the rest. We have heard that the case is pretty slanted in favour of the Department but that is another matter. The producer has since dropped his appeal. The Minister recently stated that his Department was looking for another test case. Meanwhile, Saskatoon officials of Revenue Canada have other instructions and have begun to send farmers notices of assessment.
An accountant who offered three of his clients as potential test cases was turned down with no reason given. In fact, the official said she did not care what the
June 19, 1989

Minister said in the House, Revenue Canada was going to go ahead with the assessments anyway.
Will the Minister keep his word and find another test case? Or is he afraid that the courts will rule in the producer's favour and thus stop his Department's harassment of farmers who followed Revenue Canada's rules only to find them being changed later on in the game.

subtopic: LIBERAL PARTY OF CANADA
LIBERAL PARTY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 21 the citizens of Canada spoke with foresight and clearly indicated they would not allow the Liberal Party of Canada to govern this countiy. In hindsight it was a very wise decision. The Liberal Party is a party bereft of policy and money and now a leader.
The Liberals rightfully planned a convention in Calgary to tiy to establish a policy with which the Party and maybe Canada could live. Well, they could not even let that, decision stand. The Liberal Party does not have any money so it decided to seek an arrangement with a major bank so that the Liberals could charge their expenses on Visa. Just like they ran the country, they have no idea how they are going to pay their bills.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party has announced the longest leadership campaign in their history, a campaign the Liberals want the taxpayers to pay for. For over a year this band of opposition critics bereft of policy and money will be leaderless. Can they really wait until June of 1990 to bring this group together, united under one leader who will lead a party that will still have no policy?

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking of policy, the policies of this Conservative Government are strangling the Canadian environment. I would like to refer to a specific report which was published today by Greenpeace which is a damning indictment of the Government's so-called commitment to the Montreal protocol.

The Montreal Protocol was signed by our Government as a sign of our interest in the environment, but in 10 days, the Minister himself will not have the ability to proceed with this protocol because he has not established regulations concerning CFCs.

We have a situation in this country where 25,000 refrigerators are currently being drained of CFCs. In total there are one million refrigerators between Canada and the United States. Those CFCs are not being recaptured. They are leaking right into the environment and they are going to affect the air we breathe, the drought situation in the prairie provinces and the very quality of life that Canadians hold dear. So it is fine for the Minister to sign the Montreal protocol but when he tables legislation this week, we ask him to do something about CFCs and used refrigerator appliances because otherwise all of his talk and all of his government policy is nothing more than smoke and mirrors as was stated in the Greenpeace study.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to a recent Gallup poll, almost all Canadians or approximately 97 per cent of the adult population say they are aware of the dangers of pollution. Almost three-quarters of Canadians in this age group believe that pollution is a very serious problem. In 1987, only 67 per cent of respondents shared that view. In Quebec, where the proportion of affirmative answers was the highest, four people out of five, or 81 per cent, said that their province was affected by pollution.
Mr. Speaker, the general response shows that Canadians have become increasingly aware of the dangers of pollution and that times have indeed changed. The trend indicated by this poll shows that the concern of Canadians for environmental issues has increased during the past ten years.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CAMP IPPERWASH BE CLOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Chippewa of Kettle and Stoney Point on Lake Huron have a 47-year grievance with the Department of National Defence. During the last war, the Government took over 2,000 acres of their land at Stoney Point for military purposes. Native families were forced to move but were told that they could have their land back after the war when the land was no longer needed for military purposes.
This reserve land is now used as a summer camp for cadets and no longer serves any regular military functions. However, the beautiful beach-front land is being much appreciated by military officers as a private summer camp for their families.
The Chippewa want to build houses for their people and to develop, the beach-front property so they can create jobs for the community. I call upon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight) to do the right thing, to close Camp Ipperwash, return the land to the Stoney Point people and relocate the cadet camp to another military base where it is wanted.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION
CANADA POST CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Government has been trimming and cutting and destroying the fabric of Canada Post to make a profit, Canadians have had to endure poorer and poorer service. In my riding of Parkdale-High Park, Canada Post, by threatening to close Postal Station V located at 25 Ritchie Street, has forced the residents, many of whom are elderly, to have to go four or five kilometres to get a simple registered letter or to mail a package.
Owners of small businesses that are located in the area because of mail service at Postal Station V will now have to take time from the workday to go all the way to Postal Station M to pick up a package or send a Priority Post letter. These small businesses are being attacked from all sides by this Government with respect to taxes and operating costs. Now they do not even get the mail service they need to do business.
Surely the Government has a duty and a responsibility to all Canadians to ensure the smooth running of our essential services, one of which is Canada Post. I call upon the Minister to reverse his decision and to keep Postal Station V open.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT

Mr. Speaker, recently U.S. President George Bush agreed to take long-awaited measures to drastically cut carbon emissions that have been causing serious cross-border pollutants. I commend President Bush on his historic initiative, but I would caution that more drastic measures must be taken
June 19, 1989

to control the high acid rain emissions currently being recorded.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING
GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tory Government is morally bankrupt and no amount of tinkering can change that. The Government is paying a consultant $600 every day to help sell the sales tax. The consultant says it may be immoral but it works. I say that it is immoral.
The Government allows tax deductions for those corporations or businesses that advertised for the Government on the trade deal but not for those businesses which advertised against the trade deal. That is immoral.
Three times the Government promised improvements in child care. It introduced a Bill that reduced the number of spaces, promised it again in the election but did not provide for any reasonable improvement in the Budget. That is immoral.

subtopic: FISHERIES
FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some confusion exists as to the scope and mandate of the
special committee of Cabinet announced recently under the chairmanship of the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to review implications of the apparent diminution of the northern cod stocks.
For several months now, it has been readily apparent that coastal regions of the Maritimes face serious difficulties as a result of the diminution of groundfish stocks on the Scotia-Fundy region. Nova Scotians in particular will be further hard hit if current forecasts of northern cod stocks prove to be correct inasmuch as 30 per cent of those stocks are harvested by Nova Scotian vessels including vessels from Lunenburg and Liverpool.

subsubtopic: INCREASE OF SEA LAMPREY IN GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a sea lamprey is an eel-like parasite that attaches itself to the undersides of fish and kills Lake Superior trout and salmon. Sea lamprey are found in the Great Lakes and at one time were under control, but unfortunately, insufficient funding has caused the sea lamprey to make a resurgence in Lake Superior and the other Great Lakes.
In 1987, the Government froze the level of funding for sea lamprey control. A report by provincial, state and tribal agencies of the Great Lakes estimates that the Great Lakes sea lamprey will double, trout and salmon stocks will diminish by 50 per cent, the Great Lakes sport fishing industry will lose $552 million and the commercial fishing industry will lose $135 million. In sum, the economic activity of the Great Lakes region will decline by $1.4 billion annually.
I urge the Government to alter this course. Increased program and research funding is imperative if we are to save the salmon and lake trout in Lake Superior and the other Great Lakes.

June 19, 1989

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. There are two groups of Canadians in Ottawa today to protest two of the Government's decisions linked to the Budget cuts, decisions to destroy the fabric of our country. Mayors from Ontario and Quebec are protesting the cut-backs in VIA Rail service and a grassroots group of people from Summerside, Prince Edward Island is protesting the closure of the armed forces base on the Island.
The Acting Prime Minister will know that this country is held together over vast distances by a framework we have developed as a nation for over 100 years. The country is held together by policies that treat all regions of Canada equally. The Government is tearing that fabric apart.
What did the Prime Minister mean when he campaigned in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, just a few months ago and said on October 15, "In the future, Canada will be doing more, not less for all of you"? How can the decision to close down the Summerside base gibe with the promise made by the Prime Minister of Canada two weeks before the election? What answer does the Acting Prime Minister have for the hundreds of people who have come to protest today on Parliament Hill against the closure of the base?

subtopic: PROMISE OF PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, instead of destroying what made this country great, we should provide positive support. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the sitting of the House was interrupted for the lunch break I was pointing out some alternatives that the Government might use in order to offset the deficit about which it is so concerned at the moment. I pointed out a couple of tax provisions which I thought would do two things; they would provide funding to reduce the deficit and would also help in the fight against inflation. I wanted to carry on by pointing out in the last few minutes available to me that there are alternatives. I was attempting to point out some of the other choices which the Government has to raise money and to reduce the deficit. One of the things which the Government has overlooked is where it gets its money.
Let us examine the long-term pattern of taxation with respect to the proportion of revenue accruing from personal and corporate taxes respectively. We know that in 1950 income taxes from personal and corporate sectors were approximately equal and together they represented some 75 per cent of the total federal revenues. About three-quarters of what the Government took in came from income tax, half of that from the corporate sector and half from private individuals.
By 1988, personal taxes had risen from 35 per cent to 47 per cent of total government taxation and revenues, while corporate taxes had declined from something like 40 per cent to about 9 per cent of government expenditures. In other words, the corporate sector has managed to sharply reduce its relative share of the cost of government operations to less than one-fifth that borne by individual taxpayers collectively. In 1988 terms, if the corporate sector contribution had been equal to that paid
June 19, 1989

under personal taxes, instead of a budget deficit of some $30 billion the Canadian Government would be looking at a surplus of $18.5 billion.
The difference there is quite dramatic and if the Government is really serious about reducing its deficit, one of the first things I contend it should do is start going back to equitable taxation between the corporate sector and taxation of the individual and small business.
Earlier I pointed out some of the problems that came from this kind of tax policy. Instead, the Government brought in a Budget which imposes additional taxes on individuals. It proposes to add, at the beginning of 1990, a new sales tax which, far from being revenue neutral as was touted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) months ago, according to Finance Department officials' own figures it will take an additional $3 billion from the pockets of individual taxpayers.
I contend that under any definition of inflationary pressure that will be inflationary. The Government is asking people to shell out even more money for services and will be creating an inflationary environment. The Government is feeding the Bank of Canada with a policy which is attempting to keep the Canadian dollar high by keeping interest rates high and attracting dollars to Canada, something which is self-defeating on a whole series of counts.
We heard in Question Period today that we are very close to having the first trade deficit that the country has faced in more than 50 years, all because we have built the Canadian dollar up into the low eighties from the high sixties. In order to do that the Government has successively increased the amount of interest that we have to pay.
Small business people, farmers and homeowners in my riding are having to pay ever-increasing interest rates, an increase of more than 3 percentage points over the past year.
When we produce our goods and services for export, whether it is grain, light manufactured goods or wood products, the price that we receive in U.S. dollars, whether we sell it to the United States, Asians or Europeans, the value of the product in our market is down. When we were selling it for 67 cents U.S., and are
Borrowing Authority
now selling it for 82 cents or 83 cents, the amount of money that we have to keep is very much smaller. We have lost 15 per cent to 18 per cent of the value of those products simply because the Government has decided to go for a high dollar kind of policy accompanied by high interest rates.
If the Government is serious about cutting both inflation and the deficit, a lower interest rate policy accompanied by a slightly lower dollar would help us to get there. The cost of carrying the something between $320 billion to $350 billion accumulative deficit would go down if we let the interest rate go down. The amount of money that exporters right across the country would gamer from shipping products outside of the country would go up. With those extra funds, new economic activity could be created. Instead, the Government chooses the current route of charging more taxes and reducing very much needed services to constituents.
It has particularly been hard on constituencies lying outside of the big metropolitan areas, areas like Mackenzie in Saskatchewan which I represent. We have seen a commitment in this Budget for the Government to cut $90 million to $100 million per year from its contribution to the crop insurance program. This means that the farmers and the provincial governments are going to have to pick up the difference. Given the tendency of the provincial governments of late, I predict it will mostly fall on the farmers.
From this Budget we have seen an announcement to end all branch line rehabilitation. The last little branch line in western Canada which is going to be built this year is being built into my hometown. There is 13 to 14 miles there. After that, there is no more money. What does that mean? It has been accompanied by an announcement by C.N., and apparently soon to be followed by CP, that the track crews which CN have will be cut by one-half. They are going to lay off half the workers. Anybody with seniority of under 12 or 13 years will be probably laid off and out of work. The branch lines have now been reserviced or totally abandoned. Those branch lines which have been rebuilt are only guaranteed service until the end of this decade, this century, to the year 2000. They will not need track crews any more to keep them up. They have all been rehabilitated in the last 10 years. The companies have just callously decided to lay off half the track crews and let the service go to pieces

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
because they will not be servicing a lot of these towns in the very near future. Within a decade they can abandon them. This came about because the Government decided to abandon those particular programs.
This last Budget ended interest-free cash advances to farmers which has been a part of the farm network of services for the last 15 years or so. It has now ended. There is an end to the commodity based loans under the Farm Credit Corporation where the Farm Credit Corporation is asked to share the risk of declining farm prices. They cannot do that. The Government talks a lot about the risk but they do not want to be involved in sharing some of the risks they are imposing upon Canada's farmers.
This Budget saw the elimination of the Dairy Special Export Program. It is no longer in existence after this Budget. This Budget saw the termination of the At and East grain and flour rates which permit Halifax, Quebec City and the ports which are open over winter to participate in the grain trade while the seaway is frozen up. It is being put to an end. It will reduce the potential for export. It will reduce the jobs which exist in those ports.
This Government has, in short, given up on a lot of programs that I think were necessary to keep the regions of this country healthy, and has continued with a program of leaving the regions to the mercies of the cold winds of economic rationalization. It would not be so bad if that was all the Government was doing but it is forcing this rationalization by interfering with the interest rate, interfering with the dollar, deregulating transportation and the other services which might keep these regions in business. It is doing everything it can to force them out of business. I do not know how the country can continue with that kind of policy.
