Mr. Speaker, I think it is particularly appropriate that on this day when we have the mayors of the Quebec City-Windsor corridor in Ottawa to deal with the Government's devastating cut-backs on VIA Rail and to address the environmental issues, that we also have an opportunity to speak on the borrowing Bill. The Government is seeking authority to borrow millions and millions of dollars at the same time
as it claims that it does not have the money to maintain essential services.
It is interesting to note that in one of today's columns it is pointed out that one single interest-free loan which has been recently tendered to-

-the Lavalin Corporation is worth as much as all the funds throughout Canada for all unemployed workers, whether they lost their jobs because of free trade or something else.
Mr. Speaker, it's incredible! The Government says that it does not have a cent, that it is almost broke, but when the time comes to give Lavalin an interest-free loan, it finds the money. However, when the time comes to pay for VIA Rail to make linkages among communities, it never has the money.

This Government is fraudulent in the sense that it is claiming to the people of Canada that it cannot afford to keep the rail service going. What is the ultimate effect of a cancellation of the rail service? In our own area, the Government is spending millions of dollars on an ongoing basis to try and keep traffic going into the Toronto International Airport. The Toronto International Airport at the moment is an economic disaster area. In fact, my colleague, the Member for Gatineau-La Lievre (Mr. Assad), raised a question in the House last week that conventions, conferences and business people do not even want to go to Toronto for conventions because the airport is such a disaster area.
We know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) himself, gutless though he may be-he is not prepared to admit to the public that there is a severe safety problem in Canada's skies-has undertaken a secret study of the safety issues which are basically at the root of some of the problems in Toronto. I am doing everything I can to avoid Toronto. One of the ways which we can avoid the Toronto International Airport is by using an effective train service.
The decision by this Government to eliminate VIA Rail passenger service at the very moment when we as a nation are becoming cognizant of the fact that the environmental time bomb is ticking, is sheer folly. If we look simply at the issue of the creation of sulphur dioxide and the carbon monoxide emissions from automobiles and how much our own atmosphere can be saved by effective and efficient use of passenger service, and if we believe the comments of the Brundtland Commission about sustainable development, then surely we have a responsibility to encourage the use of communal passen-

ger service. In particular, a most efficient use of the rails which are a cleaner, more effective form of movement of Canadians than the amount of fossil fuel burning which is needed to get one jet off the runway at Toronto International Airport.
When we want to talk about money and savings in the economy, let us understand that the train service in this country has formed an integral part of the development of the communities.

And, Mr. Speaker, I think that there are other issues related to the Government's decision to cut the ties between communities.

We are not just making an economic decision here. What we are making is a decision to amputate the lifeline of an island like Cape Breton.
I was in Cape Breton on Friday night and met a young student who uses the train to get to university. She told me that if that train is cut off she will not fly because she cannot afford to. The bus service makes it necessary for her to stay overnight in a hotel in order to make a connection. The train service effectively and efficiently provides a link between the island and the mainland and keeps Canada together. This is not just an economic issue, it is an issue about whether the Government believes it should be putting money into communities that link Canadians from coast to coast.
If Sir John A. Macdonald in the early 1860s had looked at the issue of the CNR, he may have said it does not make economic sense. It is too expensive. We cannot afford to do it. He could have been a doomsayer and a naysayer like the Conservatives. But instead, Sir John A. Macdonald had a dream. He had a dream that despite all the economic forces pulling us to the south we were going to build a country that went from east to west. We were going to pay the price that includes sometimes having a postal service that is not just there to make money. Did you hear the Minister responsible for the post office-I should say the coast office, because that is about what it is doing at the moment-boasting about his profit? There are thousands of Canadians in rural communities who have had their lifeline to the outside world cut off with the closure of rural post offices, Mr. Speaker. But the Minister of Regional Industrial Expan-
Borrowing Authority
sion (Mr. Andre) and the Government see the function of the post office as merely a money-making machine. There is more to Canada than sheer capital even though the Conservatives do not seem to be aware of that fact.
I was not surprised that the post office was able to report a profit. We had hearings in Hamilton recently which pointed out specifically that the post office in Hamilton is breaking the law by requiring workers to work overtime without getting paid for it. Indeed, if workers want to be hired by Canada Post they have been requested to sign a form in which they will state that they will work overtime without being paid for it. It is a violation of the law. Any business in this country could turn a profit if it were prepared to disregard the basic rights of workers under the Canada Labour Code.
We were also informed that on a regular and consistent basis Canada Post falsifies its payroll records, falsifies Priority Post recordings so that it can report that it has delivered a piece of mail on time when, in fact, it has not. That is standard operating procedure at the post office. Furthermore, we heard that it is standard operating procedure when a package valued under $100 is insured for delivery, that if the delivery date is not met there is a specific directive given to employees to destroy the contents of the package and pretend that it has been mislaid or misplaced. The post office does not want to say it has not met its delivery deadline. Anyone can cook the books, Mr. Speaker. But it is up to the Government to have a direction for this country which says that there are certain instruments of national unity which should be supported in order to build Canada east and west and make us a stronger nation.
One of those instruments is VIA Rail and its passenger rail service. Heaven knows, when the Conservatives were sitting on this side of the House we remember very well the assault on previous Liberal Ministers when they attempted to change passenger service at places like Nakina. I remember, because I myself wrote on behalf of the residents of Nakina urging CN to continue stopping in that particular community. But what we have is a deliberate and vicious attempt by Mr. Lawless-and I think his name is rather appropriate-and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to close VTA Rail. They do not want the system to work. They do not want Canadians to start using rail as an alternate, cleaner, more effective and more efficient use of common transport. They would prefer simply to shut it down. They do not look at the economy and the deficit. Take a trip down the

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
highways between the Windsor-Quebec City corridor any given day of the week.
How many hundreds of thousands and millions of dollars are lost by virtue of the fact that many of our roadways are currently impassable? They are impassable because the volume of traffic that is in a position to move from Windsor to Quebec City is far greater than the system was built to carry. If you are a trucker sitting on the highway-let us say the 401 coming east of Toronto- for two or three hours of lost trucking time multiplied by the hundreds of thousands of commercial vehicles on the road that are paying the price for an over-clogged system, that is lost gross national product. That is lost money to the economy. But the federal Government in a very shortsighted and environmentally insensitive way does not look at the long-term impact of what will happen when these hundreds of thousands of passengers pour off the trains and onto the roadways or onto airplanes.
We are spending in the millions of dollars already and we cannot deliver a decent service to fly somebody from Ottawa to Toronto. So how in heaven's name do we expect to be able to absorb the increased capacity of the number of passengers who will be leaving the trains and piling onto the roads or into planes or buses? It cannot be done. For the Government to suggest that it is merely a bottom line issue is a folly.
It is symbolic of this Government that it really does not give a dam about the regions and communities of this country that are very dependent on federal government involvement. An example of this was the response of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight) today when the people of Summerside at their own expense came thousands of kilometres to Ottawa to plead their case, and they did not even get the courtesy of a decent answer from the Minister on what research went into the decision to close down CFB Summerside. Callous, cold, cruel, uncaring, heartless are just some of the adjectives that must be used to display the utter disregard of this Government for the people of Summerside whose livelihood depends very much on the survival and sustenance of the base at Summerside. What did the Government
say? It sent out the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall).
I must say I am getting increasingly disturbed about a trend of this Government. When the Government has to make a tough decision or bring forward a tough policy, it trots out its women members and women Ministers to justify it. Well, we on this side of the House think it is unconscionable that a government that promised it was going to create hundreds of thousands of jobs is in the process of dismantling the very infrastructure that permits the survival of those jobs in those communities. What is the Minister of Employment going to say to someone in Summerside? The Minister is telling them to work together with the Minister for the strengthening of ACOA. We have seen what ACOA has done. It has built a very nice road beside the property of the Minister responsible for Nova Scotia and ACOA, the Minister who is responsible for making recommendations for ACOA. But the Government certainly does not have the capacity to replace the kind of fatal blow that has been dealt to CFB Summerside.
I do not think it is a coincidence that this vindictive action has been taken against a province that by sheer coincidence voted Liberal in the last election. There are four seats in Prince Edward Island.
The people of Prince Edward Island were not hoodwinked by the false promises of the Government and they voted Liberal. If you look in my own community of Hamilton, Mr. Speaker, we had the good sense to send three Liberal Members to Parliament. The Government is embarking on a plan which was articulated very well by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkam) who basically a few days after the election made one of the truer statements made by this Government-and I use the word advisedly-when he said that Ottawa and ridings that voted Liberal would be punished by this Government because it would not forget. Well, we are being punished in Hamilton. The Canada Centre for Occupational Health and Safety has been operating for ten years. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Corbeil) has recognized that it is a model not only for Canada but for the world. It is a model of worker, management and Government participation. Yet the edict has come down

*
June 19, 1989

from Ottawa that within the next three years, the centre must be self-sufficient or it will be cut completely loose.
To understand the mandate of the centre, one must realize that the centre makes available to workers across Canada information on chemicals, for example, materials workers may be working with which are potentially life-threatening if they spill them, rub them in their eyes or come into contact with them in an unsafe way. The centre allows them to call to find out what chemicals are involved and whether or not they represent hazards in the workplace. I dare say that some companies might make this information available to their employees but many would not prefer to do so. This service will not be able to survive because of the theory of the Conservative Party, which is that if it does not make a buck, cut it. There are some things in life that are more important than making a buck, and I happen to believe that one of them is protecting the lives of workers.
The centre was expanding to work with the Canadian environmental network on environmental information. Canadians are thirsting for information about how to do more locally and think globally in relation to the environment. The Canada Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, together with the Canadian environmental network was moving to develop a model whereby people anywhere in Canada could pick up a phone to find out the effect, for example, of CFCs, to find out what one can do in one's own home to recycle and conserve. This is the kind of useful information which could lead to the saving of our planet. That was what the centre had in mind, but because the Conservatives do not feel that the centre responds to the almighty dollar, it will cut it loose. It will kill that centre which had been operating for a decade and was visited by people and organizations from around the world.
We on this side of the House are trying to say that the role of Government is not merely to borrow money. The role of Government is not merely to create capital. The role, of Government is to create a climate in which our country is built and made strong, one which develops links from region to region. Sir John A. Macdonald had a dream that the trains could link east and west. It is
Borrowing Authority
important that the Government understand that the role of VIA Rail is not simply one of coming up with a bottom line, the role of VIA is one of linking the country.
The Post Office does not exist to make a profit. The Post Office does not exist for the trading of stocks and bonds. That is the role of the private sector, the Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal Stock Exchanges. The role of Government is to provide a base from which the private sector can grow but also to provide a base that protects the weaker regions and the weaker citizens.

The Gallup polls last week showed that the Conservative Party is losing popularity in all regions, including Quebec, the Maritimes and the West. The reason for this incredible statistic is that the Conservative Party does not understand that it is the Government's role to make this connection. All it sees, Mr. Speaker, are dollar signs.

All they can see are dollars signs popping up and down. The Minister responsible for the Post Office was practically salivating last week as he saw those dollar signs popping up and down. However, he did not talk about the increase in costs, the fact that the people in my riding cannot get door-to-door mail service if they happen to live in the newer areas and are relegated to having to use supermailboxes. He did not mention that rural post offices across Canada have been cut down and that workers are being forced to work illegally. He did not mention that Canada Post has embarked on the falsification of payroll records, an illegal activity. Those are the kinds of reports that the Government should be called to account for. Instead, all we see is the Minister responsible salivating over Canada Post's profit report.
We in the Liberal Party do not support the Government's single-minded pursuit of capitalism at the cost of the regions. We do not support the Government's pursuit of dollars through the closing down of VIA Rail and rural post offices and so many of the things that have kept Canada together. That is why we cannot support the Government's borrowing Bill. Why should we give the Government billions of dollars when it is only interested in spending the money to pump up their friends and to make the unfortunate decisions we have seen made in

Mr. Speaker, when I rose to speak on Bill C-ll at second reading on May 1, I opened my remarks by reminding Members that, in the first week of April, the Government ended its Throne Speech by stating: "May Divine Providence guide your deliberations." Since that day what we have seen from the Government will require a lot of divine guidance for us in order to continue to live with the Government for the next three and a half years.
Borrowing Authority
We have heard the discussions with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on the floor of the House and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) attempting to defend him. If this situation had taken place in Britain, there would have been no question about the route that things would have taken.
Today we are debating a borrowing Bill at third reading for more than $25 billion. During the election campaign last fall, members of the Government were going around the country bragging that they had the finances of the nation under control. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance were stating that they took on the challenge, solved it, we are on the right road and away we go. It was a real glory ride.
This winter, when the House was recalled, one of the first things we heard was that the country was facing a crisis, and our deficit was going to be bigger than expected. As a result, the national debt would continue to grow by leaps and bounds under this Government. This Government is still blaming a previous Government even though it succeeded in doubling the national debt since it took office less than five years ago. After nearly five years in office, the Government is still desperately attempting to blame someone else for not having been able to get its own act together.
Over the weekend we heard about the declining trade surplus between Canada and the United States. One does not need to have written a doctoral thesis to understand what is happening here. Months ago we told the Government what was going to happen to the softwood lumber industry in Canada when the then Minister for International Trade, the Hon. Pat Carney, slapped on a 15 per cent export tax which practically killed our softwood lumber trade with the United States. That gave the milling operations in the northern United States the opportunity to build up their mills, improve them, bring in greater production, and now they are selling under that 15 per cent protection brought on by this Government's 15 per cent penalty on our own softwood lumber industry.
The companies in the United States that we were beating into the ground as far as competition was concerned before the Memorandum of Understanding on softwood lumber, and before the free trade deal, we are now losing out to and not being able to sell our lumber. Lumber is piling up in the lumber yards of this country. There have been lay-offs across Ontario. The Government is wondering what is wrong. As far as our

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
trade surplus is concerned, lumber is one of the big sales that keeps our trade surplus in a healthy condition. Today, that has gone.
When the Memorandum of Understanding on softwood lumber was first introduced, there was a 71-cent dollar. Then the Government slapped a 15 per cent export tax on our own producers. Now the dollar is at 82 cents or 83 cents, therefore we have lost another 11 per cent or 12 per cent. The Government cannot deny responsibility for having high interest rates. I was present in the House in the early 1980s. I remember Ministers when they were in Opposition blaming the Government of the day for high interest rates in the early eighties that were as a result of world inflation and international pressures. However, today those Ministers state that it is not their fault. In the days when they were in Opposition, it was the fault of the Government. Therefore, if it was the Government's fault before, it is the Government's fault today that there is a high interest rate policy.
Those three issues have damaged the Government's surplus in trade, if it would only come to grips with it and admit a fact of life: high interest rates mean that our own industries cannot borrow money cheaply in order to upgrade facilities and compete; 15 per cent export tax on lumber; and the exchange rate on the Canadian-Ameri-can dollars.
Tbday the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Cros-bie) was once again giving the impression that everything was fine, that it certainly had nothing to do with the managerial ability of the Government that our trade surplus was declining. That is absolute balderdash. We know very well what is happening out there. The Minister for International Trade made a commitment that he was going to meet with the softwood lumber producers and come to grips with this issue and with the Memorandum of Understanding, as far as Ontario was concerned. Instead, he continues to blame the Ontario Government which was not consulted in late 1986 when the then Minister of Trade, now retired, was the one who agreed to the Memorandum of Understanding and overnight brought in that penalty on the lumber industry of this country.
The profits from Canada Post were mentioned a while ago. The Government states that Crown corporations
must pay their way. Then when Crown corporations do pay their way, the Government robs the bank, runs away with the petty cash, and uses it for its own purposes. Where is the incentive in our Crown corporations to make money today except in their dedication which is still there to a very large degree?
The Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDer-mid) appeared before the legislative committee which studied Bill C-ll. I want to make a point about that. We were sitting in a room in the West Block on Parliament Hill waiting to start the discussion on Bill C-ll, this borrowing Bill, in which the Government proposes to borrow $25.6 billion. This is not a slap against the people who appeared. They were very senior and well-informed Public Servants who appeared before the committee. Surely, as I brought out at the meeting, on a Bill of this size there should be a Minister before the committee to whom to put the political questions. We know that we cannot put political questions to senior civil servants and expect them to reply. That is the accepted rule around this place.
The Minister finally appeared part way through the meeting and answered some political questions. However, for all the information we got out of him he might as well have stayed in his office. The Minister responsible for privatization denied the fact that even though the Government was borrowing money that at the same time it was actually transferring the liabilities of the national debt, the liabilities of running the Government, to the provinces. This means less money in transfer payments to the provinces. It passed the buck to the provincial level. What can the province do then? It has less money so it has to pass the buck on to the municipalities which come under its jurisdiction. Then the municipalities have the dirty work of cutting their programs when they live with their neighbours every day right down on home base in their own individual communities. It is either that or cutting down on programs at that level all together.
Another matter that was totally swept aside and not even discussed was the fact that in the recent Budget, $8 billion of the increase in taxes is coming from average individual Canadians while $1 billion of the increase is coming from corporate Canada. Yet the Government calls this fair taxation. It calls it a fair deal. That is the idea of fairness of this Government.

With respect to the complaints about VIA Rail the Government keeps saying: "There are parts of the country which cannot get along without transportation services and we are aware of that". The way the Government has been treating rural Canada and the regions of this country indicate that it does not understand anything about it. The Government's main interest is in the bottom line. Its aim is to cut the bottom line, forget about rural Canada and bring everybody into the cities. What will the Government do when it brings all these people into the cities? The Minister responsible for privatization said very clearly at the legislative committee that the federal Government has no right to be interfering in infrastructure services such as water and sewers for municipalities. He said that that is a provincial responsibility.
If we look at the United States today we see that the Americans have been living off their capital instead of their income. What has been the result? What has been the result of not looking after their cities? The result has been that major cities such as Detroit, Chicago, New York and so on have tremendous problems in terms of water and sewage services-all types of services for their municipalities. Their cities will cost multibillion dollars to repair because they have been let go. The states cannot afford it. Municipal Governments cannot afford it any more. National Governments are the ones which can tax almost anything to get these jobs done, pay grants and part of its share to the municipalities.
When we look at this Government today we see that, indeed, it has as a federal Government taxed nearly everything in Canada. That is probably the only role in which it has been doing well. It will continue to tax nearly everything in the country-every thing and everybody. Yet the Government says: "We are not going to touch the municipal services. They are not our responsibility". They are services that affect every Canadian in everyday life. They touch every Canadian's life. It is our responsibility as well as the provinces, the many municipalities and the people in the back streets, the concessions, roads and the main streets of Canada to ensure that our facilities are kept clean and up to date.
How can we talk in the House about environment being such a fantastically important issue today and do
Borrowing Authority
our job with the environment if we are going to forget the most important thing of all? I refer to the first-class health conditions of every Canadian citizen. Of course, if there is not good water and sewage systems, then there is not good community health conditions. There is no way that we should be trying to sneak away from that.
There are other matters which I wish to mention. One is deregulation. I spoke several times on the deregulation Bill in this House when it was presented by the Government. The Government is now in trouble with it. It brought in deregulation at a time when the United States was getting out of it. I was very interested in going home on the weekend one week ago. I picked up the local Pembroke Observer and saw an editorial which rather warmed my heart. It is dated June 10 and the headline reads: "Air Deregulation Disaster, O'Brien Says". The article states:
Deregulation of the airline industry has had a major negative impact on small carriers, says Del O'Brien.
The President of Pern-Air, a local airline, he was a member of a group that spoke strongly against deregulation when the federal Government announced it would bring in the necessary legislation.
In a speech to the Pembroke Kiwanis Club this week Mr. O'Brien said deregulation has led to a monopoly position for two major carriers and to poorer service for Canadians.
Prior to deregulation major airlines handled about 76 per cent of the traffic, now two carriers control 96 per cent.
We told the Government that that is what would happen under that deregulation Bill on transportation.
Who is Del O'Brien who spoke to the Kiwanis Club in Pembroke on the deregulation of the air industry? Del O'Brien is the Conservative candidate who ran against me in 1968. At that time he was president of the Young Progressive Conservatives in Canada. He ran against me in 1974. He came to Ottawa and advised the Government what it should be doing, that it should not be going into deregulation. The Government ignored his representations as a good Conservative candidate. He was a good Conservative candidate to run against. The Government is not even listening to its own people. It goes ahead in its bull-headed way and brings something in anyway. We can see where the private, small entrepreneur trying to run an airline in the country is really behind the eight ball.
The result of this monopoly is that all regular fairs are almost exactly the same, there is only one reservation system, controlled by the big

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
boys, Air Canada and PWA Corp. which owns Canadian Airlines International and Wardair, and, warned Mr. O'Brien, we should all be concerned about the safety of air flight under deregulation.
There are a wide variety of concerns under deregulation and one of them is air service in the north. While the big carriers are choking off competition, small airlines, many of which provide important rescue flights, are being either put out of business or moving to Toronto where the action is.
As a result air service to smaller centres in northern Ontario, and other provinces, is being reduced or even cancelled.
So much for deregulation. That is a very strong message from one of the Government's own supporters and candidates.
In closing, I would be remiss if I did not put this caveat in my speech, as I always do. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp), in a letter to employees of Atomic Energy Canada Limited, said:
-let me state clearly that the federal government fully supports the
Canadian nuclear program.
On page 1 he said:
The sources for continuing the necessary level of research and
development funding are uncertain.
If AECL does not bring in a report to show how it will make money, the Government will not loan it any. At the same time, the Government is selling off its assets and good work in the form of two Crown corporations under Bill C-13, which I will speak against.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most chilling aspects of the Government's Budget and this borrowing Bill is that it has put itself in a position where it must borrow. While it is making the largest tax grab we have seen in this country, it will still have a $30 billion deficit. Furthermore, it is eliminating many of the services we have come to expect in Canada.
During the last three years, over 1,000 foreign and domestic companies changed hands in Canada. Foreign ownership and control in Canada is the greatest of any industrialized country in the world. I thank the Hon. Member for his question. He is a very valued Member of our Public Accounts Committee and is very interested in these matters. I agree with his statement about the tax grab by the Government. I said in my speech that $8 billion of the tax increases in the recent Budget have come from individual Canadians while only $1 billion in tax increases come from corporations in this country.
I am reminded of the time when the Hon. Sinclair Stevens stood up in the House to say that he was supporting the Mitel workers. He asked why we were criticizing him when he was supporting the Mitel workers.
Of course, we know how the Government supported the Mitel workers. It sold the company to a British firm, an example of what the Hon. Member talked about, and one of the first things it did was to go into my riding in Renfrew and close down the $30 million Mitel plant and lay off over 500 workers. That is an example of corporate conglomerates destroying small town Canada.
The Hon. Member mentioned the amalgamation of firms in Canada. Those companies know they have a free hand to do so under the Government because the Government encourages big business. It does not matter how large a corporation would like to get, it is encouraged to grow larger no matter what stands in its way. That is the Tory philosophy.
This was the trend in the United States during the late 1800s, which continued until Franklin Roosevelt put restrictions on major corporations. He was accused of being a Communist for doing so, but the fact is that governments must act in the best interests of the people. When big corporations and finances begin tramping over individuals, if the Government has any heart it will prevent that from happening. One way to control such corporations is with tax leverage.
If one does not have the heart to tax big corporations and would rather slap a major part of the tax on the rank and file Canadian, one would have to be in the present Government because that is what it is doing.
June 19, 1989

In order to have a fair tax system, it is necessary to tax the corporations. Only then will there be some equity in society.
The Government has the authority to impose regulations when big corporations get out of control, and certainly, with federal-provincial co-operation, that must be done in the best interests of the country when it is required.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-11 is a bill which, in short, allows the Government to borrow up to $24.8 billion. It is worrisome, Mr. Speaker, to authorize the Government to borrow such amounts when we see how the Conservative Government is managing now.
Mr. Speaker, in recent months, I have noted some problem areas that cause Canadians concern-great concern. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to relate some of these problems that are now surfacing and that cause us real concern.
I am pleased to note that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Loiselle) is here. I hope that he will be able to make some recommendations to his Government.
Mr. Speaker, just a few weeks ago, the Government was looking for about $500,000 to complete the fountains at the Canadian Museum of Civilization in my riding of Hull-Aylmer.
We must remember, Mr. Speaker, that this contract was awarded by the Government of Canada in late 1983 or early 1984. The Canadian Museum of Civilization was to cost approximately $90 million, according to estimates at the time. From the figures and estimates that we have today, Mr. Speaker, we learn that the Museum of Civilization will cost nearly $300 million, which is more that three times the estimates the Government agreed to in 1983.
What is worse, Mr. Speaker, is that after building this magnificent structure that was to open at the end of June, they had fountains installed at a cost of $5 million. Only a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, we heard that unfortunately, the fountains facing Laurier Street will not be operational when the Canadian Museum of Civilization is opened, because apparently, the Government has no money left to finish its museum project and
Borrowing Authority
is now asking, not the City of Hull but private companies to pay the cost of finishing the fountains.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is absurd that in order to finish a museum of this stature, the Government uses money from private companies without first calling for tenders.
I think there are some very serious questions that should be asked, and I think this warrants some serious discussion. I hope that my fellow Members, especially Members opposite from Quebec, will pay special attention to an item that appeared in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in April which concerns among other things the Transport Canada building. The issue has been brought up a number of times, Mr. Speaker, and I think we have given it a great deal of thought. Just a few weeks ago, a parliamentary committee asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mazankows-ki) about this question.
Once again, I would like to draw the attention of the Government to its spending on Public Works. The Government claimed capital costs totalling $200 million on page 26 of the Budget of the Minister of Finance, and I have to tell the Government that is just not true. There is no capital cost involved in construction or eventual construction for Transport Canada, for which the federal Government had called tenders and had received them in December 1988. We know, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Public Works told us last week, that the lowest tender was $234 per square metre. All it takes is a pencil to figure it out, but if you find a saving in the construction cost for the Transport Canada building, I apologize to the House.
However, the Minister of Public Works informed us that his Government has decided to stay at Place de Ville in the Campeau building, at a cost of $315 per square metre, as of 1992, for a period of seven years, while the lowest tender was $234 per square metre, which is $81 per square metre less, or $7 million less per year. And when we consider that to stay in Place de Ville, the Government must be prepared to pay the full cost of removing asbestos panels, more than $50 million, plus the cost of repairing the heating system and other costs that may exceed $60 million. When that kind of licence is given, Mr. Speaker, I think the Official Opposition has reason to be concerned and, in fact, has a duty to be

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
concerned on behalf of the Canadian people, when it sees this kind of poor management.
Mr. Speaker, these are just a few of the points I wanted to raise today, when we are being asked to approve a bill that would allow the Government to borrow $24.8 billion. If that is how the Government spends taxpayers' money, I think we are entitled to ask some serious questions, and I think the Official Opposition will certainly vote against this Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on with some of the other problems that we are having with the investment of funds in public works and also in transportation. In the Outaouais, there is Highway 50 from Masson to Lachute. The National Capital Commission, through the Department of Public Works, had agreed to pay a major part of the cost of the road network in the Outaouais within it's jurisdiction. On the other hand, the previous federal government, as part of regional development spending, had agreed to pay part of the cost of the highway network, more specifically, of Highway 50 from Masson to Lachute and on to Mirabel via Highway 13, Mr. Speaker, and as I said, this was for the purposes of regional and also, of course, economic development.
Here again, the Government of Quebec has committed itself several times, and recently, the Minister of Transport, Marc-Yvan Cote, said that the Government of Quebec would agree to pay for Highway 50 from Masson to Lachute provided the federal Government contributed substantial financial assistance. I have referred to it several times in this House, Mr. Speaker. I made several requests to the Minister of Transport for him to include it in the next federal-provincial economic development agreement. I trust that the Minister of Transport of Canada and the Minister of Transport of Quebec will be able to agree to include this important highway on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River joining the Outaouais to downtown Montreal. So I think that it is a veiy important consideration, and again, when I see such huge amounts as $24.8 billion, I would hope that the Minister of Finance could find a few cents, a few hundred thousand dollars, if not a few million, to complete the work that they have already began in past years on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River.
Mr. Speaker, we were still talking about it at noon today, and I am rather concerned that, as the Minister of Transport was telling us again today, he was still waiting for a report from VIA Rail before he would know exactly what would happen to VIA Rail. I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that today we had the mayors of large Canadian cities, including Quebec City, Windsor and some in Ontario. And it worries me when the Minister of Transport tells us that we are waiting for the report before the Government can deal with the issue and give the necessary authorizations or leave it to a fate that may be even worse than expected. I think that it is increasingly important to take account of a system that may be very expensive today when the investments that must be made in it are considered but that I think is still a system that should in future cost us less probably and be used more than it is today. It comes down to promoting it and knowing what you want to do with it! I think that our VIA Rail system at present is deficient and outdated and major investments will be needed if we want to improve it.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude with that and say to you that yes, I am certainly concerned about the way the present Government spends Canadians' money. I am even more surprised, Mr. Speaker, when we are told every day, and again today, in advertising paid for by the Government that Canadians have to tighten their belts because the deficit is around $30 billion and the debt is approaching $400 billion.
But when we see how the Government manages Canadians' money, we can be even more concerned about the management we are getting now.
I would hope, since we are at the beginning of a term-it is just a few months old-that the promises made to us, made to Canadians during the election campaign, will not all be set aside and that we won't be victims of such a striking example of Alzheimer's disease; that this Government won't forget everything that it promised now that the elections are over and that we won't see such drastic cuts in such important things as social services and unemployment insurance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very honoured to rise to speak in this particular debate. We have had five years of unprecedented increases in tax revenues. This should have resulted in balanced budgets. However, government debt has risen to more than 90 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product. Canadians believed that the Government's budget would naturally cut government spending, but what we have seen in this Budget is the same old thing. In order to maintain prosperity and influence for themselves and their friends they have
June 19, 1989

chosen to continue borrowing beyond their capacity and are making ordinary Canadians pay the bill.
Economists are saying that the Budget brings the worst of both worlds, that Government spending cuts are so weak that the deficit will actually be worse this year and there will only be a marginal reduction next year. Trying to reduce the deficit by sharply increasing taxes will increase inflation and slow growth. This will leave little room to reduce interest rates. Excuse the cliche, Mr. Speaker, because I mean it in the literal sense, but who in the world is going to have confidence in Canada now, in our dollar, in our fiscal policy, in our commitments?
Economists also say that the Government's forecast for 3 per cent growth is optimistic, that it will not be met this year and next year it will drop to 1.7 per cent. For every percentage that growth goes down, unemployment goes up, so next year is the big story and what will the Canadian public deduce when unemployment goes up over 8 per cent and interest rates go up and the deficit target cannot be met? What a loss of confidence and trust in a government responsible for the social and financial welfare of all Canadians, not only a select few.
Lack of confidence in the Canadian dollar is one thing, but it is the massive cut in foreign aid that sends the wrong message to the world that Canada does not care. Those of us on this side of the House do care and we say that if the Government wants to cut spending it should have tightened its own purse strings and not toughened its assistance to the world's hungry citizens. There was no conscience present when $360 million was cut from foreign aid. Foreign aid should have gone up 6 per cent with inflation, not cut.
Only half of the 28 government departments are even cutting staff, the rest are all hiring. The reduction of staff is half of 1 per cent. I bet the Public Service is laughing as a lot of people consider this spending to be a joke. It is really hypocritical that only four of the 28 government departments are actually planning to spend less this year than last. The Finance Minister's own Department has manoeuvred a whopping 20 per cent increase for this year.
Borrowing Authority
While the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) is cutting aid to farmers in agriculture, the Department will enjoy a 21 per cent increase. So much for a government that was allegedly worrying about big bureaucracy.
So what is this Budget all about? Let's talk about universality. The Government has eroded social programs. It has cashed in its portion of unemployment insurance for $2.9 billion. This affects all Canadians. This Budget destroys the principle of universality. The threshold of $50,000 for taxing back Old Age Security might be the magic number for today, but what about tomorrow when inflation eats away and the threshold becomes $40,000 and middle-income families will once again be paying the tab for the Tory grab.
The other universal income support program which has been abandoned is the family allowance. By 1991, with indexing included, a total of $800 million will be removed from the family allowance program. I would like to know why the Government would give a cheque to a Canadian if there is no benefit. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) says he has not denied access, and he is right, but he has denied benefit by his claw-back scheme and that is what has been ruined by his tactics. There is no more equal benefit and equal access for all Canadians. These measures are the thin edge of the wedge. Today it is the semi-rich who are affected but tomorrow it could be everyone.
The Tories have cropped regional development assistance and in the Northwest Territories they have not even considered an agency or a program to develop the northern economy. We are not part of the western diversification or any other agency. For three years northerners have been waiting for the Government to take some action, or at least to give some consideration to economic development in the north. More and more the Government is dividing this country. The gap is growing between the have and the have-not regions. The tax measures which hit those on the poverty line hardest put big business people ahead of Canada's most valuable resource.
I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, of the oil and gas development that has been taking place in the Mackenzie Valley and Delta and offshore in the Beaufort Sea since the first quarter of the century. The Canadian Arctic has potential to make Canada energy

The Northwest Territories' economy is best viewed as two quite distinct economies. Most of the non-native population live in major centres whose economies are dominated by government or resource extraction activities. Average incomes are typically very high. Unemployment is very low. Those northerners will be adversely affected by the additional personal income tax and tax on old age pensions and family allowances, even though their cost of living is about 40 per cent higher than families of the same income living in Edmonton, for instance.
Conversely, most of the 30,500 people of Inuit, Dene or Metis ancestry, almost 60 per cent of the total population, live in small, widely scattered villages where Government transfer payments and traditional harvesting activities dominate a fragile economic base and where there are few prospects for growth. Average incomes are generally low, unemployment high and social assistance a fact of everyday life.
Unemployment rates reach 50 per cent or more in some of these communities and can no longer be readily dismissed as a native preference for traditional nonwage pursuits. Hunting, fishing and trapping as a fulltime occupation, even when possible, is no longer preferred by most native young people who are fast comprising the majority of the population, if only because they cannot earn sufficient income to purchase the material goods the modem economy provides. The new unemployment insurance scheme will negatively affect most of the residents of these native communities. Hunters and trappers will be hit by higher fuel costs.
Before this Budget, the western Arctic economy as a whole appeared to be emerging from a cooling off period after the boom of the early 1980s. This modest growth will quickly come to an abrupt halt as this Government's claw-back initiatives are felt.
The new telecommunication tax affects the western Arctic residents proportionately more than residents of the rest of Canada. Communication and transportation are the two most critical services northerners depend on. Both programs are going to be taxed beyond northerners limits to meet the multitude of increases this Budget demands.
The massive cut to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is sure to mean cuts in northern programming. People in the North depend on radio for vital informa-
Borrowing Authority
tion for their safety and in many cases for their survival. Whether people are on the land, in their camps, on the trap line or driving on a remote highway, they have a radio because they need to know the weather conditions, the thickness of the ice, the current of a river, the state of the road and the temperature. Communication is not a luxury for northerners. It is an essential service, a necessity for survival. When many of the communities depend on winter roads which depend on the thickness of the ice, it is a matter of safety.
The Secretary of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development) (Ms. Campbell) did not stop with native communication. There have been cuts and reductions. There has not been any growth in the budgets that have been granted to the native communications for radio services to many of the native communities.
As far as transportation is concerned, it is the other crucial service to northerners. I have already said the land mass is about three and one-half million square kilometres.
This Budget's increase on airport taxes, aviation gasoline and fuel excise tax is going to cost northerners more than any other Canadians. Those of us who have lived in the western Arctic and who have strived to develop our resources, and realize its full potential, it is the development of the transportation systems which will open the North and give many communities a chance for fuller participation in the territorial economy.
The lack of adequate roads, airports, docks and harbours handicaps our economic growth. A better transportation system will create opportunities for mining, tourism, fishing, trade and travel between communities. Building, operating and maintaining new transportation routes and facilities will create jobs for years to come.
However, this Budget not only increases transportation for businesses and consumer costs but literally puts on the shelf future investment in transportation infrastructure. The expansion of the North's economy will be additionally crippled by the monstrous burdens which have been placed on small businesses.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a sense of gratitude to the Senate that we are having this debate. The Senate made a well-presented argument, an argument which has registered with the Government in more than one respect.
The Government is coming to the House seeking the authority to borrow with dirty hands, and perhaps one might even say with hands which are dripping with mud, particularly in environmental terms. The Government has contradicted itself on the environment and on sustainable development in so many ways that it is not fun any more.
Let us begin this brief analysis with the Speech from the Throne. One of the Government's main themes hinges on sustainable development which will be adopted as a policy thrust in the life of this session. A few weeks after the debate on the Speech from the Throne, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) came into the House with a Budget and stated that we will move ahead with important economic initiatives, including action to ensure that economic development occurs in an environmentally sound way. These are the key words of the Minister of Finance who had evidently read the Speech from the Throne and was determined to implement the spirit of the Speech from the Throne.
What has the Minister done since then? He promptly announced the closing of 12 conservation and renewable energy regional offices. As if that were not enough, he phased out the National Conservation and Alternative Energy Initiative program. As if that were not enough, he cut transfer payments to the provinces by some $340 million, possibly endangering reforestation and other joint environmental ventures.
As of today, up to six provinces are waiting for the renewal of their forestry agreements with Ottawa. Among them are Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia. As if that were not enough, having cut transfer payments to the provinces by over $300 million, the Minister cut $396 million from overseas development assistance, something which may also affect environmental programs abroad.
These measures scream out to heaven in their contrast with the proclaimed commitment of the Government to environmentally sustainable development, both in the Speech from the Throne and in the introductory speech made by the Minister of Finance in conjunction with the presentation of the Budget.
As if that were not enough, the Minister presented a document which ignored any form of tax measures, removal of tax impediments or introduction of tax incentives that would facilitate the process of embarking on this environmentally sustainable development proclaimed by the Government in the Speech from the Throne, in the Minister's introductory remarks and last year at the United Nations by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). When we looked through the Budget, we did not find any tax measures to improve accelerated capital depreciation allowances for pollution control equipment and machinery. We looked for tax incentives for industry to recycle. We looked for tax exemptions for energy efficiency. We looked for tax exemptions for conservation products and the like. We found none of them.
Having gone through that exercise, we said to ourselves that maybe the regime for cutting the deficit is so massive that it has been applied across the board in a savage manner affecting everyone and every sector and interest. We looked for an announcement that would indicate the Government's determination to find the $5 billion tied up with energy megaprojects. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that we could find any reference to energy megaprojects in the Budget? We could not find one word

about it. There are, as Hon. Members know, $5 billion tied up in the Oslo and Lloydminister projects as well as others. The application of the Budget in a selective manner which ignores the basic commitment to sustainable development is mind-boggling.
We all know that we are running out of time in relation to the question of climate warming. My colleague from Davenport explained some of the weaknesses of the Budget, be it in the foreign affairs envelope or environment. Needless to say, the record of the Government in the environment has been extremely weak, although it had a conversion like Saul did when he went to Damascus. However, nothing has really happened.
Our whole tax system has to be overhauled. It is such a complex system that no one really wants to tackle it, or else there are too many vested interests protecting the system as it is. Far be it for me to say who is right and who is wrong about the whole tax system. I am not an expert in the tax system. I guess that few people are. However, there are basic principles that were brought out many years ago by the Carter Commission which started in 1967 under the late Right Hon. John Diefen-baker. It was a a great initiative on his part that there should be a Royal Commission into the tax system. It took many years before the Carter Commission could write up its conclusions. Unfortunately, the document, as credible as it was, was never published. It was used at Harvard University and in Scandinavian countries as a basis for seeing how a comprehensive and just tax system could be implemented. The document was remarkable. I say in this House that Kenneth Carter is probably one of the unsung heroes of Canada.
The basic principles he outlined would make the tax system fair and equitable for all Canadians. However, some 25 years later, if we look at the tax system and the deficits that are being accumulated, it is obvious to any Canadian that something is drastically wrong. Nonetheless, we go on without a deep reform of the whole tax system.

Mr. Speaker, I said that about 25 years ago, a study was made of the taxation system in Canada, and that we have never really wanted to come to grips with the problem. Hon. Members opposite have heard it all before: The rich don't pay taxes! It may be just an expression, but if we look at the taxation system in Canada, there is a great deal of truth in it. Incredibly so, in fact. When we see the advantages for the financial elite in our country, we have
Borrowing Authority
to conclude that the wealthy in this country do not pay their fair share.
I believe, Madam Speaker, as the Carter Commission pointed out 25 years ago, that there is a way to be fair and equitable towards all Canadians. There is an expression that was very apt at the time, but unfortunately, it wasn't taken seriously-

Mr. Speaker, you probably remember the expression of that time: "A buck is a buck". No matter how it was earned the Government had a right to tax it. However, over the years we have seen loopholes in the law. They are loopholes that are not a mysteiy and that were dictated by the financial leaders of Canada. The Minister of Finance had to go along with some of their requests. I become impassioned on this issue. There are but a few Members of this House who have gotten up to point a finger to say that the financial elite in this country used the tax system to their benefit to the disregard of the middle class. I read a book which influenced me greatly. It is one by Linda McQuaig. She now works for The Globe and Mail. It is entitled Behind Closed Doors. It was translated into French. I have been told that it is a good translation.

The French title is La part du lion. The book shows how in the past 25 years, Ministers of Finance have been increasingly pressed to hand out tax benefits. To whom? Not to the middle class but to the financial world, which has never paid its fair share. I say the time has come to take another look at the basic principles proposed by Kenneth Carter in the report of his Royal commission of inquiry on the subject.

For anyone who is interested it is a complicated affair, that is for sure. There is no doubt that if anybody wanted to sit down and look at the tax laws obviously one would have to be a lawyer because it is so involved. However, no one can make me believe that with common sense we cannot get to the basic principles. What Canadian would not agree that the most fundamental principle in a democracy is that it would be fair and equitable? But the fact is that it is not. Is it any surprise that after all these years we have a deficit that is getting out of proportion? When we compare our population of 27 million to the United States with well over 240 million, our deficit on a

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
per capita basis is twice as high. There is no mystery that something in our system is flawed.
It is time that we woke up to this problem. I hope to see the day when the average Canadian, especially the middle class which is the backbone of this country, will ask each and every Member of Parliament what their role is to ensure that the tax system is fair and equitable. There is no other way to make it work than for the majority of people to call upon their individual representatives to sit down and find a way to make the tax system fair and equitable. We are not asking for any more.

Mr. Speaker, this has been a particular concern of mine for years, and after lunching from crisis to crises, in time we will have to take a much better look at what happens in a country with a deficit that is out of control, and realize that our tax system is far from being fair and equitable.
We should take a look at the problems we will be facing in the next few years. In only a few years, after what happened in Saint-Basile-le-Grand, the environment has become an extremely important issue. It has become the most important issue in our daily lives, and rightly so. Maybe this should have happened 20 years ago, but at least it did happen, and we are thinking about it, and we will have to keep on thinking about it. However, it is going to take a lot of political will and public funds to solve the problem in the years to come.
The other problem is municipal infrastructures. [English]
I want to deal with the question of infrastructure. We are beginning to see that as a result of years of neglect, our roads, bridges and other infrastructure are deteriorating rapidly.
A couple of years ago a professor from Cornell University estimated that the repairs to the infrastructure in the United States, which he considered to be in an alarming state of deterioration, would cost approximately $500 billion just to bring it to a reasonably safe level. A couple of weeks ago we met with the Mayor of
Quebec, who is president of the Union des municipalites de Quebec. They anticipate that they will not be able to absorb the amounts needed for the maintenance of the municipal infrastructure.

We know that in the future Canadians will be asking Parliament for this help because it is the Government of Canada that has the most powerful borrowing authority, as illustrated by this Bill in which the Government is asking for $24.8 billion, and perhaps more.
The provinces are having difficulty because of the Government's policies. They must absorb many of the expenditures and as a result of the deficit we will be in a very difficult position to help the provinces, let alone the municipalities that need assistance with their infrastructure.
I recommend Linda McQuaig's book Behind Closed Doors. While it is not gospel, it provides a basis for everyone to at least recognize that it is time for us to consider total reform. We were given a tremendous example 25 years ago and those principles still hold true today. Let us look at that again and perhaps in the years to come we will see this reform as part of the solution, along with the constraint in spending that we will have to impose upon ourselves. Perhaps we will have a just and equitable tax system for all Canadians that we can say we developed through a tremendous amount of political will and in spite of pressures against reform.

It is a major tax grab, but a tax grab which the Government said was necessary because it had to deal with the deficit. Besides the tax grab, the Government has said that it is spending far too much in certain areas and therefore it has to cut back. It is cutting back on old age security, family allowance, cutting back wherever it can. In so doing, it is changing the fabric that has made Canada the kind of country that it is.
We have on one hand a major tax grab and a major cut of services. The reason given for this change was that it was a means of dealing with the deficit. What really happened? Instead of making a major impact on the deficit, it is as high as it ever was and we continue to accumulate a considerable amount more each year, at this time probably close to $30 billion or more. In the process, we have pushed the national debt or the

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
accumulated deficit, whatever you want to call it, up to something over $300 billion. It has become a major factor in the expenditures of this country. Are we to believe that by increasing the taxes and reducing the services that this country has looked at all the possibilities of reducing the deficit, if it is so necessary to do, and the Government claims that it is.
We should perhaps talk a bit more about what I like to call the four phases of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). If you look back through the last year, you will find that the Minister of Finance and his Government-I cannot blame it all on the Minister of Finance-have had four different decisions. There was the pre-election decision which was: "We have done such a great job of the economy and in directing the country that we have no real problem. Perhaps there is a little deficit there, but let us not worry about it. We are doing so well that we do not need to worry about it. The country has turned the comer. Our policies have pushed the country around the comer. We have all of these good things that we are going to give you, such as a major child care program and drought relief. We are going to support agriculture so that farmers can be sure they are going to get some returns." All of these were part of the pre-election phase, number one.
Then the election came along, which is phase number two. "The deficit is no longer a problem. All the things that we said we were going to do and did not do because money was short, because of the bad job that the Liberals did in governing the country, because of the wastage, and all the things that the Nielsen Report was supposed to do for Canada, we are going to do. We do not have any problems any more. Just put us back into power and we will give you child care and $800 million worth of drought relief." That was phase number two.
Then we got out of that election. The Government was returned with a reduced majority, but they were returned, and we have a post-election, pre-budget period during which the Government and the Minister of Finance suddenly rediscover the deficit. The Minister told us that none of the projects that the Government had been planning and promised-remember this was the Government that had been in place before the election-to do during and before the election were possible now because all of a sudden the deficit was so
important that it could do nothing. Everything that the Government had promised during the election would have to go by the board because the deficit is so large that it has to do something about it. I told you what they did about it, they increased taxes, reduced services and increased the deficit. Face number three, the post-election, pre-Budget period.
Let us look at face number four, the Budget. What did the Minister of Finance do in the Budget? He said that we cannot afford any of these things, that we will have to step back and curtail economic growth, we will have to accept more unemployment, we will have to accept higher interest rates, we will have to curtail economic growth until it hurts. The most chilling factor is that we are still going to have a $30 billion deficit, that we are still going to push the accumulated deficit to over $300 billion, and we are still going to be paying a high interest rate on that accumulated deficit.
The reason for all of this did not go away and it is not predicted that it will go away in the next four years. Therefore we find ourselves here now debating, not the four faces of the Minister of Finance, but the result of what the Government has been doing for the last four years which was assisted in this direction by the previous Government.
The Budget is attacking universality, although I know the government side will say that they are not attacking universality, that everyone is going to get their pension and everyone is going to get their family allowance. However, they are attacking universality in the sense that old age pension, which has been considered a right by all people across Canada regardless of class or category, will be clawed back from people in a particular category.
I would think that before very long after this goes into effect someone will challenge the Government on this as it is discriminatory. If my friend from Vancouver and I each make $50,000 but part of my income comes from an old age security cheque, I will be taxed more than him. I think the time is coming when someone will challenge that and the Government is going to lose. Although this may not be a direct attack on universality, certain people will not receive retirement benefits when they reach the
June 19, 1989

age of 65. The same will happen with regard to family allowances.
We have prided ourselves over the years on putting in place a safety net for the people of Canada. That net meant that if people got sick or found themselves without a job, there would be a worth-while and effective net in place for which they had paid. That safety net is being attacked. We should be most cognizant here of the fact that this is the beginning of the attack. We cannot be secure in the knowledge that the Government will not do more next time. It attacked the universality of the Old Age Security and the family allowance. It changed the structure of unemployment insurance so that it no longer resembles the insurance that we had.
Where will this end? This should be our major concern. Will it reach the point that if you can afford it you will have to pay for the schooling of your grade school and high school-aged children? Is it going to reach the point that if you are rich enough medicare and hospitalization will be your responsibility, that the Government will not maintain that kind of a net? Will there be a further change in the attack on family allowance and Old Age Security next year so that if you earn $30,000 you will have it all clawed back and the year after that if you earn $20,000 you will have it all clawed back until no one gets Old Age Security if they are getting a minimum wage? Will it stop at unemployment insurance? We do not know where it is going to stop.
Our Party has always felt that we have a responsibility to let the Government know that it had alternatives to reduce the deficit, that it could be reducing the amount that the accumulated deficit is costing us. We do not believe that our only duty is to oppose. We believe that we should also point out the weaknesses in legislation and the alternatives available to the Government. We have a different philosophy and different ideology than does the Government or the Liberal Party. We work from a base which we believe to be the best for the people of Canada. We recognize that the ideas which we put before the Government now and in the past are good ideas. I point to the social fabric of the country as proof of that. The ideas which have built the basic social fabric of the country were ideas which our Party or our predecessors put before previous Governments. I speak
Borrowing Authority
of old age security, health care and family allowance, to name a few. Part of the social fabric of the country was formed as a result of ideas and structures which this Party put before this Parliament many years ago.
When I first came to this House, the Member for Winnipeg North Centre at that particular time, Stanley Knowles, told me, when I was very disgruntled at how little impact we were having, that we do have impact, that every one of the programs that I am now speaking about were private Members' Bills put before this Parliament 30 years ago.
The Government seems intent on tearing the social fabric which the people of Canada have put in place and supported. What can the Government do? It can do a lot. As I pointed out to one of the earlier speakers, there have been over 1,000 foreign and domestic acquisitions in Canada in the last year. Those acquisitions have done nothing to increase the number of jobs that we have. In fact, if anything, they have decreased the number of jobs.
We have in Canada the highest concentration of corporate power of any industrial country in the world. The top 1 per cent of the enterprises control almost 80 per cent of the assets in Canada. Nine families alone control 46 per cent of the value of all the shares in the largest 300 corporations in Canada that are traded on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
We have this kind of a structure in Canada. The policies of this Government are further increasing this kind of structure. Every time we allow a corporate merger or a corporate take-over, we lose. We lose, particularly if it is a foreign take-over. We also know that in the last three years we have experienced in Canada a deficit of interest and dividend payments of over $15 billion annually.
What I am talking about is that $15 billion of interest and dividends earned in Canada have left Canada to go to other nations. Fifteen billion dollars, which is half of our deficit this year. Every time we allow a merger, we increase the amount that will leave the country. Where does it end, when we are 100 per cent owned by corporations other than Canadian corporations, so that every dividend that is paid in country leaves this country

June 19, 1989
Borrowing Authority
and we become mainly a country with large and successful huge corporations which we do not own.
When the Swedish Government found that they had increased from 7 per cent to 7-1/2 per cent of their corporations foreign owned, they had a huge debate in the parliament in Sweden. The basis of that debate was, should we put in place certain restrictions which would limit the amount of foreign ownership. All of these things are ways in which this Government can start looking and dealing with the problems of deficit if it thinks it is so important that it do so.
I talked about mergers. Let us talk about one other issue in the financial structure. The Government keeps telling us that on one hand it cannot change the interest rate, that it is important that the interest rate be set by the market. The director or the president of the Bank of Canada is under the auspices of the Government, and if you do not believe it, go and ask John Diefenbaker. He made the Bank of Canada become subservient to the Parliament of Canada. This particular Government does not seem to think that that would work. If we reduce the interest rate by 1 per cent, we would reduce the deficit by $1.5 billion. We have the power to do it.
There are alternatives which this Government can look at and can use to reduce the deficit and do what it says is so important that it do. However, it is unwilling to do it because it does not direct the direction of our economy. It is done by somebody outside of the Government. Those mergers and those large corporations have more power than this Parliament.I think that is a veiy sad state of affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. It gives me the opportunity to put some of my views on record. I think that the Government in its preoccupation with deficit reduction runs the risk of throwing the baby out with the bath water. Let me try to explain that.
If we go back to the election day, November 21, 1988, what we have witnessed is an unprecedented barrage of Government propaganda. After the election was completed, the Government put its propaganda wheels in motion and those wheels have been running at unbelievably top speed ever since. Canadians are sensitized to
this matter of deficit reduction. I think that most Canadians appreciate that the deficit is a problem. However, we have to be careful. As I said earlier we cannot throw the baby out with the bath water.
Let me, if I can, touch on a couple of areas. First, the CBC, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Well, you can perhaps make fun of the CBC, but I will tell the Hon. Members, it is a fundamental service in this country. We cannot do without the CBC.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I will remind the Hon. Members, and I will remind my colleagues from Calgary and from Selkirk, that it was a Conservative Government that started the CBC, it was Tories who started the CBC. It was people like R. B. Bennett who realized that we could not run this country and this country could not survive without the CBC.
All we have to do is check the records. In fact, the late Prime Minister, the Prime Minister of that period going back more than 50 years, made some very, very eloquent speeches in defence of establishing a public broadcasting system in this country. Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? I will tell you why, because back in the 1930s when television was not around but radio was,listen to this, the Canadians in those days, yes, even Tories, were concerned about American influence. They were concerned about the incursion of American programming into this country. They decided to do something about it. They set up the CBC. It is one of the smart things which the Tories did in this country. They established the CBC.
Over the years, the CBC has done a tremendous job and established a world-wide reputation. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is known as one of the best networks, bar none, anywhere in the world. In fact, there are professionals in the broadcasting field, Mr. Speaker, who will tell you that the CBC is the best. It is not No. 2 and it is not No. 3. It is the best, even ahead of that well known famous BBC in Great Britain. That is the kind of reputation which the CBC has. It is that kind of service provided by the CBC and that kind of reputation of the CBC that is in danger now because of the cuts which are proposed in the Budget of the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of a couple of months ago. Unfortunately,
June 19, 1989

over the years, and perhaps because the CBC did such a great job, the CBC was just simply taken for granted.
For a while, back in the 1940s and 1950s before the private sector got its act going, particularly on the television side, the CBC was really the only act in town. It was really the only show in town. People just took it for granted. Now, because of the advent of private sector television and radio-and they have been in the game for a long time-the CBC needs support. It cannot be taken for granted any more. That is why those of us who are so strongly in favour of public broadcasting have come to the defence of the CBC. The CBC is an endangered species because of this Government.
Let me tell you something, Mr. Speaker. In the Budget of the Hon. Minister of Finance there are proposed cuts over the next four years neighbouring about $140 million. Do you know what that would do, Mr. Speaker? First, it would make the CBC unrecognizable. In fact, that is not my word. That is a word used often, since the Wilson Budget, by no less than the President of the CBC.
