subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FOOD AND DRUGS LABELLING OF DRUGS
speechtext:
It is my pleasure to begin this debate on more extensive ingredient labelling for the medicines we need and use in this country. I hope the debate will speed the efforts currently under way and change attitudes among interested parties who are already in constructive consultation with the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I have several people to thank for the information I have today. The staff and volunteers of the Allergy Information Association, especially the executive director Mrs. Susan Daglish, have provided me with excellent scientific information and case histories. Their organization is the only national organization which represents allergic individuals and health professionals in this field.
I also owe a great deal of my information on this subject to Dr. Ed Napke, chief of the Product Related Disease Division of the Department of Health and Welfare. Dr. Napke's work in public and professional education, scientific drug monitoring and study has probably done more to advance policy in drugs and allergies than any other Canadian scientist.
There have been other endorsements of my motion's intent from organizations and individuals across the country. The Alberta Hospital, Edmonton, especially the mental health hospital board, and the Association for Vaccine Damaged Children have been very supportive. The association drove home to me the fact that vaccines, too, are drugs and reinforced my belief that we have a long way to go in this country in helping patients and relatives make responsible decisions about the health care they receive.
As well, I should mention Jamie Lawson, parliamentary intern who is responsible for gathering much of the information for this motion today.
Drug Labelling
Without the efforts of these people I would have been unable to present to the House anything more than statistics and scientific knowledge. If we stuck to "just the facts", we would be missing some very basic facts.
The Non-Prescription Drug Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Drug Manufacturers' Association and its umbrella organization, the Federation of Canadian Health Care Associations, have all written to me endorsing the principle of full ingredient disclosure.
Here are some of the facts as seen from the consumer's point of view. Currently, voluntary guidelines request disclosure of excipients causing widespread sensitivities for non-prescription drugs. Excipients for prescription drugs need only be listed voluntarily in the professional reference work, compendium of pharmaceuticals and specialties. Many companies release no such information at all. Let us consider the occasional result.
An individual does not feel well and makes an appointment with the family doctor, then stops at the drug store to fill the prescription. After bringing it home and taking it according to the directions, the individual settles down to wait to feel better. In minutes the person begins to feel something, to feel worse than during the whole day. What is happening?
What might be going on is an adverse reaction to something the person did not even know he was taking. It is something called an excipient.
As I discovered, there are literally dozens of excipients in many medicines. They do not directly serve a healing, diagnostic or protective purpose. In some cases they are meant to be the "Mary Poppins" chemicals, the spoonful of sugar to help the medicine go down. Others hold powders together in a pill form, prevent chemical reactions and decomposition, release the medicine slowly, or make a dose easy to hold, swallow, or apply.
Some prescription creams have up to 58 such chemicals which many used to call inactive ingredients. Unlike the medicinal ingredients which are the working chemicals that make the drug worth taking, these chemicals have long been ignored by society in many respects. The best drug testing in the world focuses mostly on the drug itself, not the excipients. Drug experiments are initially aimed at healthy animals which are chemically different

June 19, 1989
Drug Labelling
from ill humans. Even the latter studies which focus on humans will not always capture the rarer reactions to the drug in combination with different living environments.
Different companies put approved drugs in completely different "chemical packages" and frequently each firm will offer certain drugs with different flavours and in different forms.
In addition, each body is chemically different. Obviously we know casually that John and Maiy are allergic to different things in different ways, but this is based in part on their different day-to-day environments in a way which is very hard to predict.
Dr. Napke pointed out:
Man is a walking test-tube. Each time a chemical is added or subtracted the balance may be upset.
He has also been quoted on the subject of how reliable even the most respected and dependable studies are, given the setting in which they take place. Testing, no matter how professional, cannot foresee all possible adverse drug reactions. This kind of perfect world is not what this motion can promise.
What this motion can promise is a way of reducing risk to patients by keeping them and their physicians better informed. It is based on the premise that consumers have a right to know what is in a product when they buy it, not just when they take it home and use it. By letting patients, physicians, and pharmacists know what is in a given pill we can make progress on several fronts.
First, people with known allergies to foods and drugs could avoid them more easily. Let me read a letter given to me by the Allergy Information Association:
I have a 16 month old child. She was tested after a year of problems, and corn is her major allergy. My baby is very underweight with all her sickness, only 22 pounds. She has had three ear problems in six weeks and I can't find an antihistamine/ decongestant she can tolerate. Most have a corn syrup base which caused a severe reaction: hyperactivity, destructiveness, irritability, colic pain, gas, crying constantly and not sleeping. The reaction took 36 hours to leave her system after I discontinued medication. Doctors and pharmacists can't help me any more and I am at a loss. Could you recommend children's medications which are com free?
As another example, there is currently a human rights case before the Ontario courts in which a woman was denied a permanent position at a firm because of a violent allergic reaction to ASA or aspirin during a
three-month probationary period. She says that she lost her job not because she was so foolish as to take aspirin but because she took a medication which contained ASA without listing its fullingredients.
Second, labelling excipients will make diagnosis of allergies much easier. In one recent case, a 36 year old man was allergic to polyethylene glycol which is added to many drugs, shaving lotions, and milk products. One day he took a normal drug just as anyone here might. Suddenly his blood pressure dropped, he lost consciousness, and he went into a seizure. He was experiencing life threatening anaphylactic shock. His doctor phoned the manufacturer which turned down his emergency request for information. The manufacturer would not even confirm that polyethylene glycol was present in the drug until the doctor threatened to list the brand name of the medication as cause of death if the patient died.
I am sure that most Canadians, including drug manufacturers, are appalled by this story. The Allergy Information Association has sent me numerous cases of allergic reactions or other medical emergencies in which time was wasted negotiating with companies to get vital ingredient information. We cannot end all of the risk, but why not end the life threatening delays and fatal errors that can be prevented?
Even with the best will in the world, the current system is costing lost hours in people's life and work, lost dollars in the Government's medical support programs, and lost lives and wasted talents in the homes and workplaces of this country.
According to the AIA at least 20,000 Canadians suffer from an allergic reaction to a drug every year. Some
5,000	Canadians per year are actually admitted to hospital mainly because of a drug reaction. In fact, 3 per cent of all acute care admissions to hospital are due to adverse drug reactions. There are also other forms of substance intolerance such as diabetic reactions to sugar filling in pills. Persons with celiac disease react to the presence of gluten, a substance found in most cereals and in such medication as capsule shells.
The general term for allergies and these other types of substance intolerance is an "adverse drug reaction", or ADR for short. In Dr. Napke's opinion, which has been both unique and influential world-wide, ADRs should include any effect of the drug, including no positive
June 19, 1989

effect at all which does not aid in curing, diagnosing or protecting the patient.
ADRs, in other words, are what happens when a drug is not just a drug, but also a foreign and potentially harmful substance. Just how frequently ADRs occur in the general population is not clear, but surveys show that they affect between 5 per cent and 35 per cent of those in hospital.
No one can say for certain precisely how important ADRs are in part because of the lack of easily accessible ingredient information in the public domain. There are not reliable figures of lost jobs, tax burden, burden on the health care, or cost to the economy. Clearly, however, based on what information exists, we are looking at an extensive as well as a tragic problem in all these areas. It is important to bear in mind that allergies produce a broad range of symptoms. These reactions can change in intensity, triggering agency or symptom. Changes may evolve slowly or after periods of stress, pregnancy, and other changes to normal hormonal balance or from poor nutrition. It is also important to stress that allergy reactions are diverse and can be confused with many different illnesses. This makes the identification of a drug allergy even more difficult.
Beyond the all too familiar and unholy trinity of asthma, stuffy nose, and rashes, reactions can include fatigue, headache, insomnia, rapid mood changes, confusion, depression, anxiety, paranoia, hyperactivity, heart palpitations, muscle aches, joint pains, hives, hay fever, bed wetting, shortness of breath, diarrhoea, eczema, abdominal pains, and constipation.
Less common are the severe reactions including psychosis, seizures, and anaphylactic shock. Dr. Marshall Mandell, an expert in clinical ecology, has recently concluded that between 50 per cent and 80 per cent of the average day-to-day medical practice are patients with allergic reactions all too often misdiagnosed. Bearing in mind the complexities of allergies, the author of an article in the summer 1987 edition of the journal Vitamin Supplement made the following observation:
One of the most important aspects of the study of allergies is the
fact that they are highly individualized.
Drug Labelling
This point is particularly significant. If chemicals put in a drug affected or killed a large part of its users, we would expect the Government's regulators to ban it. In the case of ADRs, one person's drug is another one's poison. Because ADRs are individualized government regulators must still act, but they must concentrate their efforts on helping individuals protect themselves. We have to accommodate both the needs of the non-allergic person needing medicine, without standing in the way of another person's right to defend his own life and health.
If I may, I would like to give just a brief bit of information on this issue. I introduced this motion on December 15, 1986. I made it a motion because it requires only a single vote in the House and therefore can have a quick impact. It also avoids trapping the Government into language which inadvertently makes implementation difficult or impossible.
However, on August 18, 1987 it fell prey to the old danger of being talked out. Nonetheless, the debate was helpful for two reasons. In the first case, it demonstrated that this motion could attract support from all Parties. In the second case, the matter was pursued before the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare. After further hearings into drug, food and cosmetic intolerance, the committee submitted a report and a series of detailed recommendations on July 14, 1988 and demanded a reply from the Government.
Significantly, the committee recommended an approach which included labelling, but did not restrict itself to informing the public by way of labels. I accept these developments as promising, sophisticated approaches to the complexities of drug disclosure.
However, I would prefer to see labels than accompanying pamphlets or even toll free ingredient information hot line numbers printed on the package. I feel that labelling is simple, direct, and easily accessible when the key decisions are made to buy, prescribe or use a particular prescription or non-prescription drug.
During the early part of 1988 there was also considerable evidence that the Ministry was moving toward more action in drug labelling. On January 15, 1988 information letter No. 733 was issued by the Health Protection Branch of Health and Welfare on the subject of mandatory disclosure of all drug ingredients. The due date for replies to the document was only four months thereafter.

June 19, 1989
Drug Labelling
In veiy broad terms the information letter was suggesting that all ingredients be made public in qualitative alphabetical lists on all drug labels or in accompanying lists in the case of smaller containers.
By February the Minister for Health and Welfare would cautiously testify before the House committee that the question was no longer "should something be done?", but rather "what is practical?"
In August, the first company in Canada, Searle Canada Inc., voluntarily moved to reveal its excipients to the public through labelling and publications sent to the medical community.
I want to congratulate this company for taking this initiative which has two purposes; one, it demonstrates that this can be done by a company involved in the industry if it chooses to do so and, second, it paves the way for other companies which may not have yet followed suit. This fine action was praised by representatives of the industry, the Allergy Information Association and the medical professions.
Searle is reporting that the cost factors in changing labelling were minimal. I note, Mr. Speaker, that Searle has seen fit to send a representative here today from Toronto to observe this debate.
However, Searle represents only a small fraction of the market-place and the lack of consistency throughout the market limits trustworthiness of even an expanded voluntary system. The extent of labelling, what may be withheld as a trade secret and what not, the terminology to be employed; all of these matters should be standardized if the consumer or patient is to feel confident of what is there to be read.
I would like to close my remarks on a personal note. I first thought of this motion nearly two and a half years ago. I was angry about the allergy problems of my young children, angry that my wife, our doctor and I were pretty much shooting in the dark when it came to discovering what drugs they could tolerate. We got good information about the actual medicine in the children's drugs but there was generally only sketchy information about the additives, colouring, flavouring and fillers for drugs. I knew other people had the same problem but I did not
really know how serious this issue was, how many people were affected and how complicated a solution would be.
I now feel that by approving Motion 437 which is before the House today we have the opportunity to do something very important. I urge all Members to support this motion and to take the matter forward. I hope that the Government will see fit to act quickly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by congratulating my colleague, the Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin), on his introduction of this particular motion on a subject matter which I believe is of great concern to a good number of Canadians. I want to congratulate him for seeking the consent and co-operation of other Members in terms of introducing the amendment that he started off with.
Some years ago, I believe in this Chamber, and perhaps you were here at that time, Sir, a former Prime Minister said, "Consumers have a right to know what is in a product when they buy it and not when they take it home and use it". Those were the words of the former Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
I wish to join with my colleague and support him in this particular motion which I think provides benefits to Canadians, particularly those who have a variety of diseases. There are approximately 3.5 million Canadians who are treated for allergic diseases every year, that is, one in six. Two million Canadians have hayfever, over one million have asthma, and one million are affected by other allergic conditions including eczema, hives and allergic reactions to food, medication and insect stings. Some allergic individuals suffer from more than one form of disease. Allergies tend to run in families. If one parent is allergic, the child has one in four chances of developing that allergy. If both parents are allergic it is likely that two out of three children will be allergic as well.
The question that we ought to pose is how are children in this great country of ours affected. Point five million children in this country have hayfever, .8 million children have asthma and .2 million children have eczema. Allergies may develop at any age, beginning as early as infancy. One in five children visiting doctors do so due to a major allergic disorder. Asthma is the most common cause of pediatric admissions to Canadian hospitals.
June 19, 1989

When allergic women are pregnant, approximately one-third have fever symptoms, one-third become worse and the condition of one-third remain the same way.
Those are some of the facts, Mr. Speaker. This amendment moved by my colleague from Edmonton Northwest provides good information to those Canadians who have an allergy themselves or have a child with a particular allergy.
We all know from previous debates in this House as well as in committees that the opposition presented to making these particular changes was also presented with regard to the Food and Drug Act concerning certain foods. In fact, opposition to labelling food came primarily from the food industry in other substantive matters which came before this House. I guess the same argument could be made here as well. I would like to go through those arguments briefly.
They said that labelling would reveal their secret recipes to the competition and that processing and cooking would change the protein structure of the ingredients to such a degree that the information would be meaningless. That is what they said with regard to the Food and Drug Act. They said that consumers would not utilize labelling because they would not bother to read them or, if they did, they would not understand the terms. They said that it would be costly and difficult to list ingredients on food packages. Those are only four arguments that were used.
In a non-partisan way I say that those arguments can be made with regard to the specific motion that we are dealing with. However, I think you will find that since the Act of 1969, whether it be pharmaceuticals or what have you, these particular arguments hold no water whatsoever. What is wrong with Canadian consumers having this knowledge about drugs? Surely there is nothing wrong with that kind of information being imparted to Canadian consumers and making it mandatory that the Department of National Health and Welfare have it included.
This is a very worthy motion, Mr. Speaker. I wish to congratulate my colleague again for bringing what I believe to be a substantive amendment to the attention of this House. I would like to congratulate all Members of the House from all Parties for the support that they wish to give to this particular motion.
Drug Labelling
We know that this motion is merely a proposal being made by a Member of Parliament expressing an opinion with regard to the changing of regulations. However, I think it goes to the heart of knowledge and information which we are imparting to Canadian consumers. Not only in my capacity as the official critic for National Health and Welfare for the Liberal Party of Canada, but also as a father and as a person who has been watching this particular matter for quite some time, I wish to concur with the comments made by my colleague and offer him my support for this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FOOD AND DRUGS LABELLING OF DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise in support of the motion of the Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin). I want to congratulate him on his persistence in once again bringing the subject of drug labelling to the House. He is asking us to consider the advisability of amending the food and drug regulations in order to require the labelling of all drugs, irrespective of their intended use, so as to include a quantitative list of all medicinal and non-medicinal ingredients.
In the wide array of methods utilized to improve health status, the use of prescription and non-prescription drugs has played an important role and for most people the drug prescribed and used does what it is intended to do. However, for a large number of people it causes an adverse reaction and there are two possible causes for this. It is either an adverse reaction to one or more of the active ingredients in the drug in question or to one or more of the excipient ingredients in the drug. In other words, either something which is in the drug to assist the individual with their illness causes an adverse reaction, or something which is used to enable that drug to be taken causes the adverse reaction.
The Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology estimates the extent of those in our society who have adverse reactions to a variety of substances and drugs. For example, 3.5 million Canadians are treated for allergic diseases. That is one in six of all Canadians. A million Canadians have asthma. A million Canadians are affected by other allergic conditions, including eczema, hives and allergic reactions to food, medications and so on. One in five children visiting a doctor do so due to a major allergic disorder. In hospitals, 20,000 patients suffer allergic reactions to drugs and 5,000 people enter hospital because of allergic drug reactions. While both

Drug Labelling
prescription and non-prescription drugs have provided major gains to Canadians, they also give rise to major problems for other Canadians.
Present regulations require that only the active or therapeutic ingredients of drugs be disclosed. The excipient or non-active, non therapeutic ingredients do not have to be disclosed at the present time even though there is evidence to suggest that they do in some circumstances cause adverse reactions in some people.
The motion put forward by the Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin) would require the disclosure of all ingredients, including flavours, colourants, binders, lubricants and preservatives, all ingredients of the drugs both active and inactive. All the motion asks is that consumers have the right to know what is in the prescription and non-prescription drugs they will consume. Surely, all consumers have a right to know the contents of those drugs so as to protect themselves from adverse reactions and consequences and so as to make decisions on whether or not to use the drug in question on the basis of knowledge of its content. In this way, consumers could be protected. Costs to the health system of those people who do have adverse reactions could be reduced.
A similar issue arose when regulations were put into place requiring the disclosure of ingredients of foods. The food industry was opposed to the inclusion of such ingredients on the basis, they argued, that it would reveal secret formulations of their products and that manufacturing processes changed the chemistry of ingredients so that much labelling might not be meaningful. They argued that no one read the labels. They argued that it would be costly and difficult to list the ingredients on labels. We are hearing the same sorts of concerns today from drug companies. As we have heard, though, Searle voluntarily responded to the need for disclosure, thus indicating that it cannot give rise to too large a competitive disadvantage and cost to provide that information and they should be highly congratulated for making that move.
Not only were the concerns of the food industry at the time of regulations on food products shown not to come to pass, they also did not deter the government of the day from passing the regulations in question. It is hoped on this side of the House that any concerns about the
costs and other difficulties with regard to labelling will not be affected today either and that the Government will respond to this motion which, as we all know, has the support of all sides of the House.
Consumers should have the right to know the contents of the prescription and non-prescription drugs they take. Pharmacists and members of the medical profession should know of all these ingredients too so that they can advise their patients and have some confidence in the effect of the drugs which they are to prescribe.
The information in question, which the Member for Edmonton Northwest is asking to have considered for inclusion on drug labels, is already provided to the Government in the process of drug regulation. The information, therefore, is already available and already presented in a form which could be readily translatable onto a label. We need only to ensure that that information is added to the list of active ingredients on the label of drugs which are sold in Canada.
I and my Party wholeheartedly support the motion put forward by the Member for Edmonton Northwest. Canadians have a right to know the ingredients of what they are consuming. The Government of Canada owes it to all Canadians to provide them with this information in a readable and legible form at the time they make the purchase and/or the decision to use any drug in question.
The rule, Mr. Speaker, should be disclosure of the information. As I say, I wholeheartedly support the motion put forward by the Member for Edmonton Northwest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this evening to rise in the House to speak to the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin).
Mr. Speaker, I have a personal interest in this motion, but I would also like to take this opportunity to expand on the Hon. Member's motion and say that, in addition to the therapeutic or medicinal ingredients that are needed in order to prepare the dosage form. These ingredients include, for instance, what are commonly
June 19, 1989

referred to as excipients, lubricating agents, binders, preservatives and colouring agents.
The safety of these ingredients is generally well established and the ingredients themselves are widely used in industrialized countries. However, in recent years, a small number of non-medicinal ingredients has been associated with harmful effects in a small percentage of patients with very specific allergies.
It is not always possible to eliminate or find substitutes for these non-medicinal ingredients. In some cases, the nature of the medicinal ingredient itself limits the range of non-medicinal ingredients used with it. Furthermore, the nature of the medicinal ingredient may be such that not using a certain non-medicinal ingredient may compromise the stability of the pharmaceutical preparation. It is also a fact that substitution of a non-medicinal ingredient does not guarantee that some people would not be allergic to the substitute product.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, individuals who are sensitive to certain substances need and are entitled to know the composition of any medication before taking it.
The Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare has received many inquiries from individuals, consumers' groups and health professionals, and many expressions of concern about the lack of a statement of non-medicinal ingredients in pharmaceuticals.
For many years, the food and drug regulations have required the name and amount of medicinal ingredients to be given on the label of any medication.
In recent years, representatives of the branch have worked closely with the pharmaceutical industry to determine how to inform consumers on the nature of non-medicinal ingredients in drugs.
These negotiations between government and industry have resulted in the manufacturers' associations adopting voluntary guidelines for the listing of non-medicinal ingredients. For non-prescription drugs, these guidelines specify that ingredients known to cause allergic reactions in a large number of individuals will be listed on the drug label. Since prescription products are not usually distributed to consumers in their original packaging, informa-
Drug Labelling
tion on the non-medicinal ingredients will be given to the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, which will publish it in the Compendium of Pharmaceuticals and Specialties (CPS), a publication available to physicians and pharmacists and, to a lesser extent, to consumers, in public libraries.
Although these efforts have proved useful, the concept has not been accepted by all interested parties. Furthermore, most if not all ingredients can cause allergic reactions, although very few have been found at fault. Clearly, regulatory action was necessary in order to guarantee that health professionals as well as Canadian consumers would have access to information on non-medicinal ingredients in pharmaceutical products.
In January 1988, the Health Protection Branch issued Information Letter No. 733, in which it proposed that the qualitative declaration of all non-medicinal ingredients on the labelling of drug products should be made mandatory. This Information Letter received ten times the usual response, Mr. Speaker. In fact, we received 155 letters. The vast majority of respondents, 140, were in favour of the proposal, while 35 disagreed, but only on the manner of disclosure of the information. Although alternatives to listing the ingredients on the label were suggested, none of these suggestions satisfied the consumer's need to have access to the information when and where the drug was purchased.
In July 1988, in its fourth report, the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare recommended amending the Food and Drug Regulations to require a full qualitative listing of all ingredients in all pharmaceutical products. The Department of National Health and Welfare is committed to adopting provisions requiring the declaration of non-medicinal ingredients. Provisional regulations are now being drafted and will be published in Part I of the Canada Gazette, simultaneously with the Department's response to the concerns expressed in response to Information Letter No. 733.
In order to reduce any negative economic impact of the proposed declarations on the pharmaceutical industry, it is suggested that implementation of the new provisions be delayed. Manufacturers will then be able to

June 19, 1989
Drug Labelling
change the labelling of their products as appropriate and exhaust their existing stock of labels.
Thanks to a sensible approach to the implementation of the new regulations on drug labelling, the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare will continue to fulfil its mandate, which is to protect the health and safety of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to add that Health and Welfare Canada was already considering a motion similar to the one presented by the Hon. Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin). In the spirit of parliamentary reform, the Government was pleased to let our hon. colleague present a Private Member's motion, as we did in the case of Ms. McDonald of the New Democratic Party when she was the Member for Broadview-Greenwood.
The Hon. Member, who agreed to propose an amendment to his motion so that it would meet all the Department's requirements, is to be commended for the work he has done in this respect and especially for his concern for the health of his fellow Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, health safety for all Canadians is paramount. It is a basic right. I therefore rise today to speak in favour of Private Members' Motion No. 437 as amended:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Food and Drug regulations in order to require the labelling of all drugs, irrespective of their intended use, so as to include a qualitative list of all medicinal and non-medicinal ingredients.
The past couple of decades have seen Canada at the forefront of efforts to label products for consumer safety. We now label packaged food and textiles. Today, we consider a motion to label all drugs and drug packaging similarly to include in this labelling a list of both medicinal and non-medicinal ingredients. We, in this House, have another opportunity with this motion for Canada to play a leadership role.
Allergies are a problem for millions of Canadians and for many of them the problem can be very serious, even life-threatening. Minute amounts of a substance have been known to cause sickness and even death. The key to
preventing an allergic reaction is avoidance of contact with the offending substance. Thus, it is of the utmost importance that individuals with allergies are aware of the substances to which they may be exposed.
There are two additional equally important considerations. First, a physician when cognizant of the specific ingredients in a given product is better equipped to make a timely diagnosis of an allergic reaction in a patient who is reacting adversely for the first time to that drug which has been given for some other reason.
Second, a physician is assisted in explaining a seeming inefficacy of a drug in which the action of the active ingredient is hindered or nullified by the adverse action of certain inactive ingredients in the said drug in some individuals.
Indeed, the arguments in favour of this motion are strong from the point of view of making a correct diagnosis, of evaluating an unexpected response to treatment and of preventing a medical catastrophe.
It may be argued that labelling would reveal secret ingredients to competitors; that consumers would not take the time to read the labels even if they were there; and that it would be costly and/or difficult to list ingredients on the packaging for medications.
I suggest that trade secrets ought to be subservient to consumer safety; that those with a life-threatening allergy to a substance would be diligent and take the time to read the labels; and that costs of such labelling would be minimal while the benefits would be substantial for those with known allergies.
A basic principle in patient care is informed consent. Also, knowledge by a medical doctor of all ingredients in any pharmaceutical agent taken by a patient or individual ensures the doctor's proper action in case of an emergent, adverse or untoward reaction to that pharmaceutical agent. Thus, giving those who suffer from allergies the knowledge required to make safe and wise choices of drugs is a societal obligation. Giving physicians all the information will enhance the delivery of exemplary health care to all Canadians.
Thus, today I speak in favour of a change to the regulations of the Food and Drugs Act to provide for the mandatory labelling of non-therapeutic ingredients in medications.
June 19, 1989

I congratulate my colleague the Hon. Member for Edmonton Northwest (Mr. Dorin) for introducing this excellent motion. Indeed, I am privileged to add my own and my Party's support to this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond to the motion that has been put forward by the Hon. Member with respect to the labelling of pharmaceuticals. This is a current initiative within the Department of National Health and Welfare and I welcome the opportunity to advise the House of the progress it has made in this area to date.
I would like to address this motion in relation to preventive health care. The issue of drug labelling of non-medicinal ingredients has been a priority in the Department for some time. Non-medicinal ingredients are not normally associated with any action on the taking of a medication for the first time. However, in recent years the health professions and the regulatory agencies have noted that some individuals are intolerant or experience adverse reactions ranging from mild to severe, including several forms of allergy.
The reactions that have been reported have varied considerably. They can range from relatively minor skin rashes to generalized symptoms of fatigue, nervousness and headache to more serious gastrointestinal or neurological effects and may even result, as some Hon. Members have mentioned, in shock or death. The responsible agent is only rarely identified.
A finite number of substances used as non-medicinal ingredients in drug products are known to cause adverse reactions in sensitive individuals. A few examples of these are lactose, a commonly used filler in pharmaceutical products, the yellow colouring agent, tartrazine, sodium metabilsulphite and related compounds used as antioxidants to preserve flavour and prevent decomposition, benzoates and parabens commonly used as preservatives and gluten, a protein found in certain types of starch which must be avoided by those suffering from celiac disease.
It is evident that although only a small proportion of Canadians appear to have adverse symptoms from some ingredients, the range of reported effects is very broad. It is also clear that such ingredients are widely used in
Drug Labelling
society without any discernible problems for most Canadians.
Drug products contain non-medicinal ingredients to perform various functions related to the quality, safety and effectiveness of these products. For example, nonmedicinal ingredients may hold a tablet together or maintain the sterility of the product. They may contribute to the rapid release of the medication after ingestion or maintain the potency of the medication within the drug product. It is readily evident that the complete elimination of non-medicinal ingredients is not possible for all products.
Since non-medicinal ingredients are essential to the availability of safe and effective drug products, it is necessary to minimize the exposure of individuals to non-medicinal ingredients to which they know they are intolerant or allergic. The initial response of the Department of National Health and Welfare to these concerns was to solicit the voluntary support of the pharmaceutical industry. As a result, drug manufacturers' associations adopted voluntary guidelines for the disclosure of potentially harmful non-medicinal ingredients.
Prescription drug manufacturers chose to declare the content of those non-medicinal ingredients that have been clearly associated with symptoms of intolerance or allergy in some people. This information was given to the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association for inclusion in the drug monographs of the reference textbook, the Compendium of Pharmaceuticals and Specialties, commonly known as the CPS. Non-prescription drug manufacturers disclose the presence of selected non-medicinal ingredients known to cause allergic reactions on product labelling.
While these efforts have been helpful, voluntary labelling and other voluntary declarations have not been universally accepted. It is also apparent that there are many non-medicinal ingredients which have the potential to cause sensitivity or allergic effects. Only full label disclosure will eliminate the continuing debates over whether a particular ingredient is a sensitizing agent and should be declared. To that end, the Department of National Health and Welfare published Information Letter No. 733 soliciting comments on a regulatory proposal to require the listing of all ingredients on the

June 19, 1989
Drug Labelling
labels of all drug products. The responses to this regulatory initiative are currently being evaluated.
Some of the issues that will be reviewed prior to the preparation of regulatory amendments include quantitative as well as qualitative declaration of non-medicinal ingredients, a consistent method of declaration on the product labels, particularly with regard to the nomenclature of the non-medicinal ingredients, exemptions of certain types of products from the requirement to declare non-medicinal ingredients on their product labels and appropriate implementation of the regulatory requirements to minimize the economic impact on pharmaceutical manufacturers and on society.
Regulatory amendments will be drafted with consideration of these and other comments received. The Health Protection Branch, with the co-operation and commitment of the pharmaceutical industry, will continue its efforts to safeguard the health and safety of Canadians by providing the ingredient information needed for the informed use of drug products.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the House on the issue of labelling of drug products in Canada and to apprise the House of recent regulatory initiatives taken by the Department of National Health and Welfare in this area.
The Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, as part of its mandate to protect the health and safety of Canadians, has the responsibility to regulate and evaluate the labelling of all drug products. It has been a requirement of the food and drug regulations for many years that a quantitative listing of all medicinal ingredients be displayed on the labels of all drug products.
In recent years, concerns have been expressed by both consumers and health professionals on the lack of information available about the non-medicinal ingredients included in those products.
This information is especially vital to those who suffer from sensitivities to certain substances. Although the majority of Canadians are not affected by non-medicinal ingredients in drugs, some individuals experience reactions which can range from mild to incapacitating in effect.
The Health Protection Branch recognizes the special needs of those individuals who are sensitive to non-medicinal ingredients in drug products. In response to that concern, Information Letter No. 733 was issued in January, 1988, to seek a uniform and practical approach to the full disclosure of those ingredients. The informa-
Borrowing Authority
tion letter proposed that the food and drug regulations be amended to require the qualitative declaration of all non-medicinal ingredients on the labelling of drug products.
Responses to the information letter were received from pharmaceutical manufacturers, industry associations, health advocacy groups, health professional associations and individuals. The principle of disclosure of non-medicinal ingredients received overwhelming, if not unanimous, support.

speechtext:
Our position, to be serious for a moment because this is a very serious matter, is that the banks have been gouging their customers for years on service charges. There is so much gouging going on that the Canadian public rose up and started to complain about this. Complaints came from everywhere, including from the Chairman of the Finance Committee.
The Government set up a special committee to look into changes to the Bank Act to deal with these bank service charges. The committee reported and, unfortu-

Bank Act
nately, the Bill had no teeth when it came back to the House.
This Bill is the same as Bill C-140 which died on the Order Paper just before the last federal election, though small business is included in this Bill. We in the NDP opposed Bill C-140 and we are also opposed to this legislation.
We oppose this Bill for a number of reasons. The Bill provides few guarantees for customers and small business against unfair service charges and does nothing to keep fees and increases under control. Hon. Members will recall a famous National Film Board short movie which won an award years ago. It was a cartoon about a person who went into a bank and was terrified. Things have not changed very much. People are not terrified of going into banks, but they are still getting ripped off while the banks are making immense profits and are the most protected of industries in Canada. Not for them wild competition, not for them the free market. They want to be protected and they also want to be able to charge as much as they can possibly get away with. They have certainly got away with a lot, and they will continue to get away with a lot after this Bill becomes law.
The Government laboured and brought forward this mouse of a Bill. The principle is that the banks can be trusted to keep service charges in line. In other words, they will self-regulate themselves. The Government took that same position on interest charges on credit cards. The charges came down a little bit when Parliament put a lot of pressure on the banks, and as soon as Parliament recessed the interest charges climbed back up. We say that one cannot trust voluntary compliance through the banks on the matter of service charges, and that is the first weakness in the Bill.
The second weakness in the Bill is that there are a number of charges that the Bill does not remove, which it could remove, such as charges for deposits and withdrawals, charges for cashing NSF cheques, charges for closing accounts, charges for maintaining a minimum balance, charges for providing the current balance on an account, and charges for errors made by the bank. The banks make an error, and you pay. You close your account, you pay. You don't have the right minimum balance, you pay.
We also object to the self-monitoring provisions in the Bill. I will address that in a moment. Hopefully, if I have time at the end of my speech, I will add some positive measures that could be taken in the House to oppose gouging by the banks on service charges.
First, the weakness in the Bill and the concept of voluntary compliance. The legislation does not force the banks to do anything about their service fees, except have them disclose the charges and notify their customers about increases or new fees. I gather the philosophy is, if the customers do not like it, they can go to another bank. Except, the problem is that the other bank will have the same service charges and fees.
In the case of small businesses, banks are not required to disclose all the charges, but only those defined as a "core list".
The Government bases this approach on the assumption that the disclosure and notification of charges will open up competition. This does little for a customer who has a mortgage or a small business that has a loan with a bank. They cannot just walk out of that bank. They would have no option but to accept the increases because it would cost them too much to transfer their loan or their mortgage.
In terms of voluntary compliance, the banks' past record has not been good. By all accounts, 1988 was a banner year for the banks. The Royal Bank had a net income of more than $700 million; the Bank of Nova Scotia's income was $506 million; and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce had record earnings of $591 million. Despite those huge earnings, the banks did not hesitate to raise service charges. The Royal Bank raised 15 of its service fees on November 1 by 4 per cent to 6 per cent, with the cost of writing an NSF cheque going up 12 per cent. I am not condoning writing NSF cheques, and certainly would not do it myself-not knowingly, anyway, Mr. Speaker. However, the charges are excessive for that accident happening, which does happen to the majority of people.
In 1987 the five major banks collected more than $1 billion from bank service charges. We need to ask then, can we really trust the banks to voluntarily keep their service charges in line, which this Bill does?
I mentioned some of the charges that are put on that this Bill does not remove, which could be removed. The Bill does not prohibit those charges, for example, for closing an account, for maintaining a minimum balance, and so on. We should have legislation that forces the

banks to provide a basic no-frills account which would provide basic services free of service charges. The banks are making enough money from investment of our money that they could afford to do this. The recommendation for a no-frills account was a central feature of a study of service charges conducted by the Finance Committee in the spring of 1988.
I mentioned self-monitoring of banks. If customers are not happy with the way complaints are made to banks, they can contact the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions in Ottawa. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions looks good on paper, but the problem is that it is not a real guarantee at all. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions may have a big name, but he or she does not have a mandate to protect consumers. In fact, the Office of the Superintendent is there to ensure that financial institutions remain solvent, not to be an appeal as an ombudsperson on bank service charges.
This Bill will only create more pressures for an agency that is already overworked. More important, the Superintendent's job is to ensure that banks stay in business, not that they satisfy customers. It is possible to imagine how those two interests could conflict.
What are we proposing, because one has to be positive as well as negative? We would accept the recommendations of the Finance Committee, such as to require the provision of free basic banking services. That is the basic no-frills service, to prohibit certain unfair charges such as the minimum balance charge and the charge-back for cashing an NSF cheque. We would agree to those recommendations; however, they do not go far enough.
In addition to what the Finance Committee proposed, we would propose a freeze on all bank service charges for one year. Why? Well, service charges have increased over the past five years at an annual rate of 19 per cent. The banks are making $1 billion a year from those bank charges. An argument can be made that the banks have over-charged consumers and should be prepared to give customers a break for one year.
There have been precedents where federally regulated corporations have been required to compensate consum-
Bank Act
ers when over-charging is demonstrated. For example, the CRTC has made a number of rulings vis-a-vis Bell Canada where consumers have received money back from Bell.
We would suggest the establishment of a financial services ombudsperson empowered to perform consumer advocacy, referee and long-term policy advice with the banks. This office would be an independent entity with a toll-free number in order that consumers across Canada could call with complaints. We live in the modem world, and that could be done. It would also advise Parliament regularly on consumer relations in relation to financial services.
The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has tabled a private Member's Bill in this Parliament to implement the recommendations of the Finance Committee and to implement the proposal of a one-year freeze and a financial services ombudsperson. The Hon. Member's Bill would extend those guarantees to all customers and small businesses. His Bill would set up a no-frills account that would not have charges for deposits and withdrawals, for cashing an NSF cheque, or for maintaining an account. Second, a personal account will not charge customers for deposits and withdrawals, for maintaining a minimum balance, for cashing NSF cheques, for closing an account, or for errors made by the bank. Third, there would be a freeze on bank service charges for one year. Fourth, it would create a financial services ombudsperson.
These are positive recommendations that would bring some justice for consumers. The banks have made a lot of money in over-charging and gouging people on service charges. It is about time that we took concrete action. We do not know why the Government is not doing that. There is public pressure from consumers for a fair shake here. The banks have been making a pile. They are heavily protected in the Canadian environment. It is not a free-market economy for them. They get together and do their thing and fix service charges. It is no accident that they all have the same policies. There is not going to be competition there. We need more teeth in this Bill. This is not half a loaf, it is about a tenth of a loaf. We want the whole loaf.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to address the proposed amendment to the Bank Act, specifically Bill C-9 and its corresponding regulations.
The Bill was introduced to the House of Commons on April 13, 1989, by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Loiselle) and was the result of extensive reviews conducted by the House Standing Committee on Finance during 1988.
This Bill, as we are all aware, is the second effort of the Government to introduce legislative changes respecting banking service charges. The first effort, Bill C-140, having died on the Order Paper due to the fall election, was similar in content to the present Bill before us. There are some minor modifications, the dominant one being the introduction of business deposit accounts in the legislation. That is the basic difference between these two proposals.
Although Bill C-9 does address some of the concerns expressed by organizations such as chartered banks, consumer advocate groups, banking associations, trust companies, credit unions, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the Minister of Corporate Affairs, the legislation falls short of adequately addressing all concerns expressed by these groups. Indeed, the legislation falls short of proposing many of the recommendations of the House of the Commons Standing Committee on Finance.
Bank Act
Perhaps the Bill could be viewed as a good start, but certainly it is not complete in its approach to the governance of banks in Canada. There are a number of areas in which the proposed legislation is deficient.
I wish to take this opportunity to review these concerns, concerns that are not only mine but also those expressed by business, citizens and bank organizations. I bring these matters forward in the hope that Hon. Members opposite will agree with the importance of these concerns and make some serious effort to amend Bill C-9 prior to its final passage so that these matters will be adequately addressed.
Bill C-9 reduces the need for banks to disclose to both personal and business deposit account holders the various charges for services rendered by the bank. Further, the Bill and, in turn, its regulations provide guidelines for the timing of disclosures of charges.
Although this is a much needed introduction, it does not go far enough to provide specific details to be followed by banks for such disclosures. The banks have argued that due to various types of accounts it would not be possible simply to place signs in branches advising the charges of the bank. The proposal would permit the use of brochures to advise account holders of various service charges. The question remains: Does the banking system need to be so complicated that it is not possible for the banks to provide simple instructions to its customers? Is it necessary to produce volumes of brochures on service charges? If the sign method is too complicated, how do banks intend to keep the brochure method an easier way of disclosing service charges?
The Bill and its accompanying regulations should specify the form of disclosure required to comply with the legislation. According to this legislation, we would permit the banks to draft and circulate their own brochures on this very important matter. If it is our intention to provide the understanding of bank service charges and if it is our intention to ensure quantity of this information, then surely it must also be our intention to ensure quality of the information to Canadians. We will not be able to achieve the goals for improved disclosure to individuals if we are not ready to regulate the disclosure content to ensure the information is frank and honest.

June 19, 1989
The legislation is silent on the issue of charging penalties against individuals and businesses for depositing non-sufficient funds cheques.
Although the banks have recently been more willing to accept the concept of no penalties for NSF cheques on personal accounts, they are still reluctant to waive the penalties in such instances on business accounts. I am sure we must all agree that when either the individual or a business accepts a cheque, the recipient should not be penalized because the cheque has not been issued in good faith and turns out to be NSF. One may suggest it is only a nominal charge, about $10, but this impacts on the individual finances as well as on business profits. In some cases, the service charge can be equal to or almost as much as the cheque itself.
Let us take the example provided to me by a newspaper delivery boy in a town in my area. I recognize that newspaper boys and girls are not big business, but in the particular instance that happened a year ago, this newspaper boy accepted a cheque for payment of a few weeks of delivery. The cheque itself, barely over $10 in value, was returned NSF. The boy was charged a $10 service fee and the bank saw nothing wrong with the system. Its response was that this was its policy.
It was only after rigorous intervention on behalf of the youth that the bank waived the service fee. Certainly it is not the intention of our bank system to unjustly penalize persons or businesses who accept cheques in good faith. Certainly it is not the intention of our institutions to introduce our youth to a business world that would have no compassion or understanding for an individual who works hard for his money only to find out that he or she can be penalized for trusting people.
Where is the bank's responsibilities in these cases? All persons and all businesses utilize banking services. Indeed, any financial transaction will undoubtedly include a bank customer. We encourage the use of banking institutions and services in our society. In return for providing these services the banks are compensated, and compensated quite handsomely. Chartered banks are recording record profits that are supplemented by fees generated by service charges. Yet they are reluctant to
Bank Act
waive the penalty against the innocent depositors for non-sufficient fund cheques.
The legislation must be altered to address the most discriminatoiy practice. Legislation must include a prohibition for all depositors of NSF cheques from penalty. This is the only fair and equitable method of addressing the issue.
At the time of introduction of Bill C-9, the Minister indicated that the responsibility for handling complaints must first rest with the financial institutions. The Bill and its corresponding regulations provide for the establishing of a complaints procedure, which calls for banks to handle complaints first.
Only after exhausting this procedure would the complainant be permitted to apply to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. However, neither the Bill nor its regulations stipulate the method which the bank must follow in processing complaints. There is no guideline or timeframe. In short, there is no guarantee that the complaint would be handled in an orderly and expeditious manner. The Bill simply requires the bank to file its complaint procedure with the Superintendent.
If the banks are provided with the opportunity to be first to deal with complaints, should the legislation not provide the guidelines to be followed? Is it not possible, with the current proposal, for banks to introduce lengthy arbitrary appeal processes? I believe it is possible.
Further, if it is our intention to make this process more simple and understandable, it would certainly be more advantageous for all parties to uniformly apply a complaints system. Therefore, I ask the Government to reconsider this issue, acknowledge the problems that could arise as a result of a Bill not providing sufficient direction in the complaints process, and introduce changes before final passage that would ensure uniform, prompt and sufficient procedures for customer complaints.
Bill C-9 in its present form attempts to address the very serious matters of disclosure of bank service charges and complaints system. The Bill is silent with respect to NSF cheque penalty charges. The Bill only addresses banks, pursuant to the Bank Act, and those banks are listed on schedules 1 and 2 of the Act.
June 19, 1989

What about other financial institutions that deal in deposit accounts, such as credit unions, the trust companies and the loan companies? What about governing these financial institutions?
Again, in pursuit of uniform and equitable legislation governing deposit accounts, service charges and complaints procedures, it must surely be argued that the rules must apply equally to all financial institutions. To this end, would it not be advisable to introduce legislation that covers all financial institutions? The banks, trust companies and co-operatives should all operate under similar guidelines.
Certainly, the Canadian Bankers Association would welcome the introduction of legislation to govern trust and loan companies and co-operatives. These institutions should certainly not be given an advantage over chartered banks by being permitted to operate by different rules.
I suggest that it would be prudent for the Government to not only strengthen this legislation as it relates to banks, but also to introduce further legislation that will address service charges, NSF cheques and complaint processes for the rest of the Afinancial services industry.
In summary, I wish to emphasize the importance of the issues raised in Bill C-9 and its corresponding regulations, and to further emphasize the need for the Government to reconsider certain provisions of the proposed legislation. Action is necessary to strengthen this legislation and extend it to cover all financial institutions.
If we are in doubt of the serious nature of banking service charges and its importance to the business community, let me refer to the Federation of Independent Business, an item, Small Business Views the Banks, The Bottom Line, edition 1988:
The issue of service charges has risen quickly to become the single most significant concern of one in every four small businesses in Canada. There is no doubt that the banks are relying more and more on service fees as a profit source. This is explained by the banks as a result of the fact that "less low cost money on account is now available for banks to lend out to other customers; depositors prefer term deposits et cetera to non-interest bearing accounts." In summary it seems that small firms are seeing their service charges increasing at rates far above the rate of inflation, and often more than once a year, with no compensation gains in other areas.

The House of Commons Finance Committee itself made specific recommendations with respect to service charges. Recommendations based on the hearings conducted in 1988 included the elimination of certain types of charges and the modification of other charges. An example is the charge for not maintaining a minimum balance in accounts. Such a charge penalizes low-income Canadians when account balances dip below the magic minimum balance figure that is established by the bank. This relatively new practice of levying a maintenance fee was a special concern of the committee. The Bill does not address this matter.
The negative response to the proposed legislation's lack of addressing the NSF cheque situation was evident in the Consumers Association of Canada response:
The Association welcomed the alacrity with which the service charge legislation was re-introduced, but said it hoped the Finance Department would have gotten even tougher with the banks-(the association) was disappointed the draft legislation wasn't tougher. Although banks may have no difficulty in complying with Bill C-9 because "banks were already complying with what was proposed in the 1988 draft legislation", there is concern among members of the Canadian Bankers Association and its comments bear this in mind:
The Banks believe they are capable of regulating themselves and do not need such legislation. We are generally satisfied - The Canadian Bankers Association believed that similar rules should be introduced to cover the rest of financial services industry, including trust companies and loan companies and co-operatives, which were also subject of last years public hearings.
The Government has seen fit to introduce service charge legislation. Bill C-9, in its current form commences the much needed overhauling of the system. What the Bill lacks is clearer, more defined policies with respect to disclosure of charges and complaints procedures and elimination of certain charges. What the Bill does not do is extend its proposals to all financial institutions.
I would further suggest that in order to assist the Government in these matters, the Bill be referred to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance. This committee, because of its previous review of the Act and its recommendations in 1988, is very capable of

Bank Act
reviewing the Bill and making further recommendations on this issue.
In order to address these matters, in order to eliminate the discrepancies to the Bill that are not solved in the proposed amendment, in order to treat all Canadians fairly, in order to treat all financial institutions equally, I request the Government to amend the proposed legislation prior to the final passage. I ask this Government to undertake these changes expeditiously and present to the House and the people of Canada a comprehensive piece of legislation that will meet our financial needs today and in the years to come, that will instil customer confidence in our banking and financial service industry.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to take part in the debate on this legislation which is a Bill to amend the Bank Act in Canada. The Hon. Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Loiselle)said in his contribution to this debate on April 26 on page 979 of Hansard that Bill C-9:
-responds to the many recommendations put forth by the Standing
Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
Indeed this Bill did adopt some of the committee's recommendations. Why though did the Government not see fit to incorporate all of the committee's recommendations which make good sense, are fair to all Canadians, and would improve the content of this Bill considerably from its present form?
Let me refer specifically to these recommendations. The first recommendation of the committee's report to the House on May 31 suggested that banks and other federally regulated financial institutions be required to provide accounts that would make basic banking services available. For these basic accounts no charges shall be levied for maintenance of the account, making a limited number of deposits into or withdrawals, or payments by cheque on the account, providing the current balance of the account and transferring to the basic account the
Bank Act
balance of any other account of the customer with the financial institution.
Surely Canadians should be able to expect that the most basic services provided by financial institutions, as cited in the recommendations, be provided free of cost. Such an amendment would ensure that poorer families, infrequent users of the bank, young children and indeed our senior citizens, who are less likely to conduct or require more complex financial transactions, can satisfy their more limited banking needs free of charge in the six banks that control banking in this country.
The current Bill fails to address this issue. More important, Bill C-9 ignores the committee's second recommendation that financial institutions be prohibited from levying charges for a variety of services. For example, recommendation 2(D) states that financial institutions be prohibited from levying charges for any transaction which results from an error or unauthorized action by the bank.
Does it not make good sense that if a financial institution makes a mistake that the cost of that mistake is not incurred by the customer? It should be incurred by the bank. Why should such a recommendation not be adopted by the Government? Why also does this Bill not prohibit charges for closing accounts, inactive accounts, or maintaining a savings account when the balance falls below the amount specified by the bank? It is curious that these salient recommendations, which would undoubtedly be in the best interests of Canadian bank customers, were not included in the new legislation which is before the House today.
Perhaps the Hon. Minister of State for Finance would respond that these recommendations would be inconsistent with his government's position, that as he stated in this House competition, not regulation, is the best way to guarantee a fair and reasonable approach to establishing prices. Have you ever heard anything so foolish, Mr. Speaker? It insults the intelligence to think that competition among the six banks in this country is going to regulate these affairs rather than regulation.
This reasoning ignores two very important facts. First, it assumes that bank customers ought to have the right to be charged for services rendered by the financial institution. It suggests that competition will establish fair prices for the customer while not ensuring that no charges will be levied on certain services. It does not exclude the possibility, but it is highly unlikely, that a financial institution will voluntarily eliminate service charges.

June 19, 1989
Bank Act
Second, perhaps more important, this is a "big city" perspective. What sort of competitive market forces does the Minister expect will come into play in small towns and rural Canada?
In many areas of my riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon there is either a single or perhaps no financial institution at all. How would competition instead of regulation do anything to help many of the residents in northern Ontario, and in fact many sections of northern Canada? The provisions of this Bill intend to allow banks to have access to the costs associated with conducting their financial transaction at that institution. In theory this will allow a customer to select which bank provides the services sought by the individual or business at the lowest cost.
This might hold true in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal or Winnipeg, but what are the implications for places such as Nipigon, Hurkett, Red Rock or Armstrong? This legislation does little or nothing for these communities. In fact, Armstrong, Ontario, a community of over 2,000 people 200 miles away from Thunder Bay has absolutely no financial institution at all and there and in many other areas there is little room for dissatisfaction with our financial institutions. In the smaller communities in northern Ontario the code which applies is usually "What you see is what you get".
Moreover, this legislation offers nothing to the many communities across Canada, and there are several in my riding, which desperately require the establishment of a financial institution. A Bill meant to increase competitiveness between banks will not assist these small places in northern Ontario.
It could be argued that increasing competition between financial institutions and prompting them to lower service charges will decrease their income, hence further reduce their incentive to set up comparatively more costly branches in rural communities. I would not find it surprising if such considerations were never given any thought by the Government. After all, in the name of competition, or more accurately, ignorance, the Government has also decided to abandon VIA Rail passenger service, shut down rural post offices, and deregulate air travel, reducing the quality and quantity of flights to rural and small town Canada. The Government is one thing, it is consistent in its disregard for northern Ontario. More important, the Government is consistent
in its complete disregard for rural and small town Canada.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business concurs that increased competition will have a negative effect on small towns in Canada. It argues that since banks are now pursuing much larger accounts, because of deregulation, profit margins on big business lendings have been decreased. As a result, financial institutions are imposing larger and more numerous charges on small businesses. Greater competition has forced financial institutions to undertake cost-saving measures such as closing branches in small towns, leaving small businesses in the community without financial institutions with which to deal.
We in the Official Opposition are also very concerned about the need now to penalize businesses or persons who deposit a non-sufficient funds cheque into accounts. In its report to the House the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs stated: "It seems unfair to penalize someone who accepts a cheque in good faith and does not receive payment from the person who wrote the cheque. There may be other reasons why a cheque is returned unpaid, such as errors. The committee is of the view that those who issue cheques should be responsible for ensuring that payment follows. A depositor of a cheque should generally be assumed to act in good faith, and there should be no double penalty for one single error". Such a proposal makes good sense, especially for small businesses. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business is adamant that there should be no penalty imposed on the person who deposits the NSF cheque.
Does it seem fair that the owner of a small business with limited resources and facilities for verification is not only stuck with an NSF cheque but that a penalty must be paid as well for depositing such a cheque in this financial institution? It makes very little sense. Reason would dictate that the individual issuing such a cheque would be fully responsible and incur whatever penalties or costs there may be and it would be up to the financial institution to impose that charge.
As a result of this intervention I hope that the Government will consider its position with respect to rural and small-town Canada and its financial institutions. I hope it would consider its position with respect to seniors and the services that they should expect from our banking institutions, and consider its position with re-

spect to our young children and bring the necessary changes in the Bank Act before this House for approval.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FARM MARKETING BOARDS-DISCOUNT OF FARM MARKET QUOTAS
AGRICULTURE-FARM MARKETING BOARDS-DISCOUNT OF FARM MARKET QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 21 put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) concerning a document which I had received from the Royal Bank of Canada. This resulted from the Government's action to freeze the income of Canadian farmers at the GATT. The decision was made and the Minister of Agriculture announced on April 14 that the Government was taking away the power of the Canadian Dairy Commission to raise the price of Canadian dairy products.
I do not think with regard to products going into international trade that there was a lot of dissatisfaction with this in the dairy industry because we are part of a global community in that regard. Farmers are concerned that their income is going to be frozen until 1991 on commodities which are used domestically. As a result of the Government's decision which was announced on April 14, the Royal Bank issued a memorandum to all of its lending institutions in the Ontario region saying they were concerned that the Canadian Marketing Boards and quotas would become a sacrificial lamb in the GATT negotiations.
We know that the Board of Directors of the Royal Bank of Canada and other large banking institutions are very close to the Government, and close to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). They obviously have a lot more information on this than the average Member in the House of Commons. This memorandum to all the Royal Bank branches is especially pertinent and of great concern to the Canadian dairy industry.
The Board of Directors go on to say that because the risk is so great of the whole marketing board structure being lost, they were withdrawing immediately 50 per cent of the value of quotas for the dairy industry and other supply-management industries for calculation of
Adjournment Debate
debt-equity ratios. They also went on to say that no quotas would be financed over a five-year period and that it would be necessary in some cases for branches to raise interest rates.
I asked the Minister of Agriculture why he was moving in this way, what was going on and what assistance and support would be provided to these producers who were losing in some cases 50 per cent of the value of their quotas for loan purposes.
The Minister really gave very little response. I was disheartened with that because this is a real problem for dairy producers across this country who want to renew or take out a new loan having the value of their quotas discounted by 50 per cent as far as providing equity in equity-loan ratios. I think the responsibility is on the Government. The Tories campaigned hard and long last fall saying that supply-management and marketing boards would be protected under the free trade deal, under the GATT deal, and yet supply-management and marketing boards are really under the gun as a result of the Government's actions. Clearly, it is not only the decision at the GATT to freeze farmers' incomes in 1991, it is the challenge which has been launched by the United States import controls which have been placed on yoghurt and ice cream. That issue, even though it has since gone into a free trade area with the United States, now challenges the right of the Government of Canada to impose import controls on milk constituents like yoghurt and ice cream. That subject is now at the GATT.
I am told that the chance of Canada winning that challenge is something less than a 50-50 chance. We not only have the prospect of larger imports from the United States with the tariff being removed over the next several years but also import controls not being effective at controlling those milk products coming from the U.S. The dairy industry has a great concern over this. The dairy farmers of Canada have published a long document in which they refute all the arguments the Government has made with regard to their position on the whole question of the dairy industry supply-management.
This Thursday morning in room 362 East Block, we will be holding a public forum in which we will give an opportunity to dairy farmers from across Canada to make presentations and express their concerns to the Government about how serious the matter is as a result of the Government's action, both in the free trade negotiations with the United States and the decision to
