freeze farmers' incomes for the next 20 months until 1991.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FARM MARKETING BOARDS-DISCOUNT OF FARM MARKET QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski). My understanding of the situation is that the Ontario district of the Royal Bank has decided to value quotas at 50 per cent of their face value rather than at full value, as it has done in the past when assessing the risk of loans to producers of supply-managed commodities. Lenders often discount the expected market value of assets based on their assessment of the marketability of those assets.
In Ontario, a recent court decision limits the security value of quota based on interpretation of the Provincial Marketing Act. This clearly has nothing to do with federal Government trade policy.
I wish to thank the Hon. Member for his concerns about farm market quotas. The Hon. Member has cited an internal document from the Royal Bank outlining changes to its lending policies on quota as evidence that federal trade policy is destroying Canada's supply-management systems. A representative of the Royal Bank has stated that the language used in the circular was inflammatory and should not have been used.
The Government has never waivered in its support of supply-management. We stood by this commitment when the Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement was negotiated and we continue to stand by it in the GATT negotiations.
As the Hon. Member knows, Article 11 of the GATT gives Canada the right to operate supply-management systems. We want to strengthen and clarify our Article 11 to guarantee this right over the long term. Because of the nature of GATT, however, we cannot negotiate this one article by itself. We would achieve nothing if we did not co-operate with other GATT members in a full review of the agreement.
The recent short-term measures agreed to in Geneva represent a necessary starting point for long-term negotiations on GATT rules for agricultural trade, including Article 11. During the course of negotiations, Canada and other countries have agreed not to raise any support prices to producers which are set above international market levels. These measures may not be perfectly fair
by country or commodity, but they are necessary to launch long-term negotiations.
Our national dairy policy does not operate in isolation from the rest of the world. There has been recognition in this round of talks that domestic support programs can lead to international trade distortion, so some shortterm adjustments may be required to guarantee a favourable long-term outcome.
It is unfortunate that these short-term measures and their impact on our dairy industry have been misinterpreted. We do not know yet what the latest cost of production data for industrial milk will show. Therefore, we do not know if the short-term measures will have any impact on the price of industrial milk.
The Government has been generous and flexible with dairy producers in the past. The target price for industrial milk is now $46.06 per hectolitre. It has remained at that level since February 1988, even though the cost of production formula indicated decreases on August 1, 1988, and February 1, 1989.
We have maintained the existing price because we were aware that drought was affecting feed costs in parts of the country. I can assure Members that banks do not set prices for milk quota. The value of the quota is set by producers based on what they are willing to pay for it. In Ontario, the average cost of buying dairy quota represents less than 7 per cent of the total farm assets. Therefore, the rest of the dairy farm assets are available as collateral if borrowing is required.
The Government remains committed to working with dairy producers and processors. It is the continuing co-operation of all participants that best assures the long-term success of Canada's dairy industry.

I brought to his attention the fact that one of the major
June 19, 1989

trains out of the maritime provinces, the Atlantic Limited from Halifax to Montreal, was a well utilized train.
The important thing to recognize at this juncture in our efforts to attempt to address the deficit, which indeed we as Atlantic Canadians are no less prepared than any other Canadian to accept our responsibility for, is the fact that the rail transportation system in our nation has been something that we have long recognized in Atlantic Canada as one of the necessary links for us as Canadians to identify ourselves with in the rest of the nation.
This nation was forged on the system of the railway transportation links. In Atlantic Canada, it is not only a matter of building up our highway system or replacing one mode of transportation with another, as the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. Thompson) has repeatedly pointed out to the House of Commons. For a great many people in Atlantic Canada, it is the only communication link with members of the family who might have moved west because of varying economic reasons, or whatever the happenstance may be that they found it necessary to move to other parts of Canada.
I want to bring to the attention of the Minister, who rightly recognizes the concern of a mounting deficit on the part of rail transportation, that as responsible Canadians we must live up to our responsibility to future generations and address the mounting deficits. There has to be a continuity of our association in Atlantic Canada with the rest of Canada, and it cannot be arbitrarily cut off by a discontinuation of what we in Atlantic Canada have grown to accept as part of our historic relation to confederation.
I know you will relate to that, Mr. Speaker, being a westerner. To succeeding generations of Canadians who have grown up and travelled from one sea to the other, the rail communication links have meant a whole lot in our ability to relate to one another as Canadians. Indeed, no one on this side of the House would suggest that we continue with rail transportation links that are not well utilized, or where there are realistic alternative means of transportation.
Adjournment Debate
I want to hasten to add that road transportation from Atlantic Canada, the Maritimes, to Upper Canada is not a realistic alternative from our perspective. Indeed, it is recognized that in the Maritime provinces there is a population of approximately 1.7 million people and that in the two major transportation links, rail transportation and water transportation, there was in excess of 475,000 people who travelled just last year. That number is growing every year. Indeed, it represents far more than the figure of 3 per cent of the population that the Government often uses as an example of the few who are utilizing the rail transportation link.
It is with that in mind that I try to reinforce that in Atlantic Canada the number of people who utilize the main rail transportation link between that part of the country and the rest of the nation is far in excess of the 3 per cent figure. Practically half a million people in relationship to a population of 1.7 million in the Maritime provinces use that link. The majority of those are not from Upper Canada but are Maritimers who are travelling students, elderly people, people with no alternate means of transportation and individuals who want to continue their links with the rest of Canada. They depend on that rail transportation system to identify with the rest of Canada as being Canadians from Atlantic Canada. I want to reinforce that it is of no small consequence to those of us who live in the Maritime provinces. It is important that we recognize that there is a substantial number of Maritimers who depend upon that rail transportation system as being their support, their raison d'etre, for maintaining their identity as Canadians in this great dominion of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) for speaking out on behalf of the Atlantic region, which region he represents as a Member of this place.
As he knows, on May 3, 1989, VIA was asked to prepare and submit by June 30,1989, a new business plan that represents its new budget. This business plan will set out a course of action that sets out the budget realities. The new reference levels which decrease gradually from $541 million in 1989-90 to $250 million in 1993-94 reflect the Government's commitment to expenditure reduction and restraint.

June 19, 1989
Options which the Government expects the corporation to consider in developing its plan include productivity improvements, fare increases, the takeover of services by other interested parties, service reductions and route abandonments. No options are being ruled out. The one restriction that has been placed on such options is that rail passenger services to truly isolated communities along remote routes will be maintained.
As my colleague, the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) has stated, no decisions have been taken on the long-term future of rail passenger services in Canada. The impact of the new VIA budget cannot be determined until we hear from VIA with its new revised plan. Once thing is clear, however, these subsidies have been disproportionately large when compared to other modes. Last year alone they reached an unprecedented $641 million. This has been due to a large extent to the low level of VIA ridership. Rail passenger services

The air mode has a market share of 7 per cent. The automobile enjoys the lion's share of the market at 84 per cent, demonstrating Canadians' love affair with their cars.
